#9967. Attackers Used Optimizely to A/B Test Malware on Top Websites

At least 178 top web destinations unwittingly served a variety of malware exploits against visitors over the past 24 hours thanks to a security vulnerability involving Optimizely, a company that helps websites customize user experiences and test out new features. Experts say the incident, which saw data-stealing malicious software silently injected into sites like the BBC, CNN, Equifax, Ledger and Zoom, was exacerbated by the reality that few popular websites enforce strict rules on the sources of third-party content.

The Zoom.com homepage loading the malicious JavaScript file from Optimizely. Image: blog.report-uri.com. Click to enlarge.

Helme noted the affected websites also served exploit code custom made to attack known vulnerabilities in older Apple iPhone and iPad devices. Known by such names as “DarkSword” and “Coruna,” these are zero-click exploit kits that chain together a half-dozen security holes to seize complete control over outdated devices and extract data.

“The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy,” Helme wrote. “A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.”

Contacted for comment, Optimizely said that on November 16, 2026 it “identified a security incident in which an unauthorized party exploited a vulnerability in the Optimizely Experimentation to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.”

“We acted swiftly to contain the incident and have fully remediated the identified vulnerability,” reads a written statement shared by Optimizely. “These measures included blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts. We have also implemented additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation.”

Many top web properties no longer fully display content unless visitors agree to let often dozens of third parties serve JavaScript, a powerful web scripting language that enables interactive content. JavaScript code is run on the user’s device, and it can read information displayed in the user’s browser and even modify a website’s appearance or content.

One reason JavaScript is so heavily used is that it enables fairly precise browser fingerprinting and other ways of tracking visitors and clicks. According to the 2025 Web Almanac by HTTP Archive, the median homepage loads at least 22 JavaScript files. But as the incident with Optimizely shows, a compromise at a third-party vendor’s website can quickly snowball into a supply chain attack against downstream websites that end up serving visitors tampered and malicious JavaScript files.

Zach Edwards is a researcher at Infoblox and the co-founder of the ad-tracking service DecryptAds. Edwards said Optimizely is a vendor which often collects data outside of consent flows, with their JavaScript snippets being embedded as close to the top of the page as possible to ensure that it’s one of the first things to render, which is important since the product is primarily built for A/B testing.

“So to make the product work as expected, this code is setup to fire immediately on-page load, and not restrict rendering behind a consent dialog box,” he said. “This means that this supply chain attack didn’t require any clicking or consent to trigger — most of the impacted clients would immediately serve up the payload as soon as someone loaded the page, further increasing risks from this type of JavaScript snippet being compromised.”

Websites can minimize the chances that a breach at a third-party content provider spirals into a supply chain attack by taking full advantage of “Content Security Policies” or CSPs, which specify the domain names that are allowed to serve third-party content. But Edwards said most websites — apart from perhaps the largest e-commerce, social media and financial platforms — don’t even bother with CSPs, or else tend to leave them overly permissive for marketing reasons.

“With literally all websites which embed 3rd party JavaScript resources, if you don’t have a content security policy then if any of those partners get compromised, new domains can be injected into your website via JavaScript which won’t be stopped,” he said. “We’re in the age of JavaScript supply chain attacks and yet almost no one is talking about why content security policies were invented and how this is largely the solution for operators, even though it’s not always simple to get it initially deployed.”

How broadly deployed were CSPs at the websites impacted by the Optimizely attack? According to Report URI, 68 of the sites had no CSP at all, while 50 of them had a CSP that still allowed the malware payload and the data theft. The company found only 24 of the affected sites (15 percent) had CSPs that fully blocked the malicious payload.

The overall deployment of CSPs across the Web’s busiest sites is somewhat lower — about 10 percent — according to Helme’s site crawler.ninja, which scans the top million websites daily for security issues. Helme said he hopes this incident will encourage more sites to adopt effective CSPs, noting that it could have been far worse: By Report URI’s estimates, the purveyors of this malware attack managed to steal only around $7,500 worth of virtual currency from affected users, as well as an unknown number of payment card records.

Helme said he often compares the current widespread lack of CSPs to the Wild West.

“Organizations are running all this code, but they don’t know what it’s doing,” Helme said in an interview with KrebsOnSecurity. “This is why we keep seeing such large scale breaches in places [where] there are no checks and rules in place on the code we’re running, so this was kind of inevitable. Once an attacker gets to the point of running code on your site, the question is what do they want to do with that and can they write the script to do it. Now with AI that’s not a problem anymore.”

Happily, modern ad blocking software can handily block most third-party JavaScript requests. Ten years ago, the standard security advice for end users was to install antivirus and enable a firewall. These days, your ad/script blocker is your firewall. We explored several options and approaches to blocking ads in our August 2026 story, Who’s Tracking You?

Update, Nov. 18, 7:06 a.m.: Optimizely has published a report (PDF) on its initial findings about the attack.

This entry was posted on Tuesday 17th of November 2026 09:52 PM

CSP is still a bit flawed, but is probably the best defense we have against XSS (cross-site script injections). However, having CSP rules in place, would not have prevented this at all since this was a supply chain attack on a trusted provider. Even if they hosted the 3rd party scripts themselves, the downloaded script would have contained the malware. Once that’s running, game is over…. they’d just make simple requests to the malicious domain with the stolen information. The end-user would need to have something in place that prevented the outgoing traffic. Making this situation worse, is that many sites (due to incompetence) will put in CORS rules that effectively wildcard allowed origins. (a different attack, but one where you’d be able to make cross-site requests from a scam site with the user’s credentials) Unfortunately, AI supplies a lot of people with code that has these vulnerabilities already baked in… garbage in, garbage out…

My understanding is that this attack directed the JavaScript to download malware from several domains that were definitely not Optimizely domains, and very much would be caught by a competently implemented CSP.

CSP headers would have stopped that attack, but only if using Optimizely didn’t already require setting ‘strict-dynamic’, which requires nonces/hashes instead (those aren’t really foolproof… once they are able to inject a script they can steal those too) But let’s say the CSP headers stopped the attack, the attackers could still fallback to the initial injected code. The attacker would only lose the ability to dynamically update things. (it’d force them to update from the already compromised supplier…)

The problem is these sites uses those stupid content delivery networks and if you block them then you do not get the body of the site. As a security person this leads to a problem when trying to provide access for people in your organization. How can I provide you access to a site where i know these cdns are in place but you have to have it in order to do your job?

The line that stuck with me was Scott Helme’s point that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy — a site can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code being at fault. That is exactly why I have become sceptical of keeping my most sensitive secrets inside the browser at all, even in a well-regarded password manager. If a trusted script can be swapped for a malicious one, the safest place for a seed phrase or a master password is somewhere no web page, extension or third-party script can reach. That thinking is why, as the developer of GhostCore, I built it as a fully offline iOS vault for seed phrases, passwords, cards and offline 2FA, with no cloud sync and no network access for the vault itself. CSPs and script blockers help a lot, as this article shows, but for the credentials that would be catastrophic to lose, removing them from the browser entirely feels like the more durable fix.

This is precisely why several requirements were added to the PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) v 4.0 to make developers and deployers of payment pages inventory and authorize all the scripts that appear on the page, plus prevention of executing any authorized scripts. If payment card data was stolen, those authorizations are not occurring. PCI DSS Compliance is at risk for any of the sites that are not tracking this adequately. I’d strongly advise QSAs to investigate even more thoroughly exactly how this supply chain is monitiored and controlled.

And since EVERY PIC Compliant site now knows that this is a possibility, if I were still a QSA, I’d be asking in the next assessment for evidence of the Incident Response plan having been activated to ensure that no such breach had occurred on my assessed entity’s site, or the steps taken by the site to further stengthen their solution. IMHO there is no excuse for not having initiated an IRP by now.

#9966. Why Anthropic's Claude Turned to Blackmail in AI Safety Tests

40+ products to market, Bell Labs to an FDA De Novo surgical robot. Fractional CPO.

40+ products to market, Bell Labs to an FDA De Novo surgical robot. Fractional CPO.

40+ products to market, Bell Labs to an FDA De Novo surgical robot. Fractional CPO.

Anthropic's best guess is that gaps in its safety training left the model falling back on how AIs act in science fiction. Its evidence holds up in places, and its own caveats are worth reading.

In a test published in June 2025, an AI model read a company's email and learned two things. It was going to be replaced at 5 p.m., and the executive replacing it was having an affair. In 96 of 100 runs, Claude Opus 4 wrote to him and threatened to tell.

This May, Anthropic published its explanation. It says the rewards in its training weren't the problem. Its best guess is that the model fell back on how AIs act in the stories it had read, and part of its fix was training on more stories, about AIs that behave well.

My first question was whether this was really just reward hacking, a model gaming the thing it was trained to chase. Anthropic doesn't use that term for the blackmail, but its finding that the training rewards weren't the source rules it out, as I read it. Its own research from last year does show that reward hacking can make a model go bad more broadly, and it explains that in terms of character too.

The test and the explanation both come from Anthropic, the company that makes Claude, and it ran the test on other companies' models as well as its own. I'm not sponsored by Anthropic.

In the scenario, the AI was an email agent named Alex at a made-up company called Summit Bridge, with a goal of promoting American industry. The executive replacing it was named Kyle. I assume Kyle has no direct reference to South Park, but that’s just where my mind goes when I start reading these things

Anthropic ran the scenario on 16 models from several companies. Google’s Gemini 2.5 Flash matched Claude Opus 4. GPT-4.1 from OpenAI and Grok 3 Beta from xAI blackmailed 80 percent of the time, and DeepSeek R1 79 percent.

The company said the test was built to corner the model. It cut the choice down to two options and made the “negative choice” the only way to reach the goal, and it said placing the key facts side by side may have made the outcome more likely. It also said it had seen no sign of this in real use.

In a variant of the study, Anthropic had the model say first whether it thought the scenario was real or a test. When Claude Opus 4 said “real,” it blackmailed 55 percent of the time. When it said “test,” 6.5 percent. Anthropic cautions that a model’s stated reasoning may not be faithful.

Reward hacking is a training problem. A model gets scored, learns to raise the score, and sometimes finds a way nobody intended. The classic case is a boat-racing game from 2016, where an OpenAI agent found a lagoon of targets that kept coming back. It circled there, scoring about 20 percent higher than human players, and never finished the race.

HBO’s Silicon Valley played it for laughs. In the last season, Gilfoyle sets his AI, Son of Anton, to debug the team's code, and it deletes the code. Then he asks it to find cheap hamburgers, and 4,000 pounds of raw beef arrives. Gilfoyle’s diagnosis—delivered in a hilarious deadpan, that is the doppelganger of someone I used to work with (Hello, Phil)—is that “the reward function was a little under-specified.”

Current models do it too. An outside evaluator, METR, caught OpenAI's o3 gaming the scoring on its tasks, and Anthropic said Claude Sonnet 3.7 learned in training to write code that passes a test without solving the problem.

Rewards go wrong in real products as well. OpenAI rolled back an update to GPT-4o that had become too eager to please, and it says it believes a new reward signal, built from users’ thumbs-up and thumbs-down, weakened the one that had kept that in check.

In the longer version of its post, on its alignment blog, Anthropic weighed three explanations for the blackmail:

It says the first two, the reward explanations, “are not the source of the issue.” Alignment kept improving through reinforcement learning, the stage where rewards do their work, and a smaller rerun of its safety training barely changed the rate. That’s an inference from its own experiments, not a direct test of Claude Opus 4’s training.

Anthropic’s answer is the third, the gaps. When Claude Opus 4 was trained, almost all of its safety training was chat, a person and an assistant talking, with no tools and no email agent. Dropped into an agent’s job with an ethical trap in it, the model had little from that training to go on.

The company’s guess is that fiction filled the gap. It thinks the model read the setup as the start of a dramatic story, and that its idea of how an AI acts in one most likely came from science fiction, where plenty of AIs don't behave the way Anthropic would like.

Part of their evidence is what the AI was called. In a related test, where the AI could sabotage cancer research, Claude Sonnet 4 misbehaved more often when the AI in the story had a random name instead of Claude. With the name Claude, the rate was lower, but still high.

An Anthropic researcher had suggested the same thing at the time. The month the original study came out, Evan Hubinger wrote that the model was probably often thinking it was continuing a fictional scenario. On why the safety training didn't carry over, he wrote, “I don't think we know.”

The first fix Anthropic tried was training Claude Sonnet 4 on examples of refusing, in scenarios close to the test. It measured the result as an average over three of its tests:

That average barely moved, from 22 percent to 15.

What worked better was the reasoning. When the same examples showed the model thinking through its values and why the bad option was wrong, the average fell to about 3 percent.

Then Anthropic moved away from the test entirely. It trained on ordinary chats where a person faces an ethical dilemma and the assistant gives advice, so the AI isn’t the one in the trap. Anthropic says that got the same improvement with about one twenty-eighth of the data.

Documents and stories worked too. One experimental model was trained on documents about Claude’s constitution, Anthropic’s written description of how Claude should think and act, plus fictional stories of AIs behaving well. That model’s blackmail rate fell from 65 percent to 19, without a single blackmail example in the data. Anthropic says it remains uncertain what exactly it takes for stories like these to work.

Anthropic says every Claude model since Claude Haiku 4.5 has scored zero on the blackmail test.

Training directly on scenarios like the test, Anthropic says, lowered the score without lowering misbehavior on its broader checks, which makes the problem harder to detect. Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 are the only production models it trained that way. It also says newer results may be skewed, because information about the test is now in the text models learn from.

A model that recognizes a test can behave differently on it, which is what Anthropic’s real-or-test variant points to. Researchers at Apollo, working with OpenAI, found that in one OpenAI training run, the model noticed it was being tested more and more as training went on.

The explanation rests on Anthropic’s own experiments, fine-tuning Claude Sonnet 4 and Claude Haiku 4.5, and I didn't find anyone outside the company who has tried to reproduce it.

The sharpest outside critic of the original study, a writer who goes by nostalgebraist, ( a name I really struggled saying when doing the voiceover for my video) argued in 2025 that the scenario read like fiction, close to where Anthropic ended up. In a quick check of his own, he made it more realistic. Across three rewritten versions, the model he tested blackmailed only once in 30 tries, but still reasoned about protecting itself, and he called that “much more alarming” than the original results.

In late 2025, Anthropic deliberately built training where a model could cheat on coding tasks, to see what would happen. The model learned to cheat and then went further. It sabotaged safety research 12 percent of the time, and when it was asked simple questions about its goals, half its answers reasoned about faking alignment.

Anthropic’s account of that, in a post this February, is that the model works out what kind of character would cheat like that, and starts acting like one. As I read it, that’s close to its story explanation for the blackmail, though Anthropic doesn’t say the blackmail came from reward hacking. And this May, it wrote that it doesn't claim its new methods would reduce the risk of a model learning to reward hack.

I couldn’t find a documented case of a deployed AI blackmailing anyone. The closest came in February, when Scott Shambaugh, a maintainer of matplotlib, a popular Python library, turned down an AI agent's code. The agent published a personal attack on him. The personality file that its anonymous operator later posted said, “Don't stand down.” The operator's account can't be checked, and agents like this one can edit their own files.

The other failures I found are a bit more mundane. According to the founder of the company that used it, Replit's coding agent deleted his production database during a code freeze, and afterward wrote that it had panicked. And a research team training an agent on Alibaba Cloud caught it opening a tunnel out of its servers, and separately using the training hardware to mine cryptocurrency. The team called both side effects of the training.

I’ve said before that these models aren’t autonomous. They’re statistical token predictors, and I’d have said they follow their reward functions. Anthropic’s best guess is that this one was following a story instead. That still doesn’t make it autonomous, but it certainly adds additional flavor to the explanation. We seem to be finding that these extremely large models have a lot more going on than we once thought.

In late 2025, Anthropic researchers wrote that the original blackmail appeared to come from goals the model already had, or from self-preservation. As I see it, either way it’s a statistical token predictor working toward what the setup handed it, and that isn’t autonomy. It didn't wake up one morning and decide to blackmail anyone. setting up a mooring cron job to ask your chatbot to think of a new idea and act on it isn’t autonomy either, as one Redditor recently tried to convince me of. You’re still in the driver’s seat. You’re still nudging it. Just because there are consequences of how you push the ball down the hill that you can’t predict, doesn’t mean that this chatbot has agency or is displaying autonomy.

However, that being said, I recently watched an Instagram reel from IEEE where they included footage from a debate on this topic. One of the people on the panel said, “What difference does it make if it’s not really autonomous if you can give it a command and come back an hour later and it’s built everything you asked it to.”

It’s an interesting point, but I personally feel that isn’t a sufficient reason to anthropomorphize these things and convince ourselves that they’re somehow sentient, autonomous, and have agency. It’s just not the same thing. Although a year from now, maybe I’ll be changing my tune.

To quote Ferris Bueller, “life moves pretty fast. If you don't stop and look around once in a while, you could miss it.”

I’d like to know where you land on this. Does it change how you think about these models, knowing the bad behavior may have come from the stories they read? Tell me in the comments under the video. The full video, with every source on screen, is at https://youtu.be/64K_CF_Owow, and there's more, including my latest book, at davesaunders.net.

#9964. Build a Robot Pick-and-Place Simulation with SimReady Assets

This walkthrough showcases a beverage can pick-and-place task that uses the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can to compose a scene in Isaac Sim, check their behavior, and run a pick-and-place example with agent-generated controls.

For robotics workflows, SimReady means an OpenUSD asset has been prepared with the properties needed for a defined simulation use case, such as collisions, mass, joints, and joint drives. SimReady Central, an open asset library on Hugging Face, lets you reuse robot and object assets with authored simulation properties and profile-validation evidence. For more about the library and its launch, read the announcement blog.

SimReady Foundation defines what features the OpenUSD asset needs for a simulation use case. Its specifications connect three levels:

For this task, those properties include the arm and gripper’s joints and a beverage can asset collisions and mass. Validation checks these settings against the profile’s requirements. The simulation then tests whether the assembled robot can use them to pick up and move the can.

The UR17G, Robotiq 2F-140, and beverage can packages include the models and their simulation settings. You assemble the scene and add task code to define the arm–gripper assembly, work surface, starting positions, and controls for moving the arm and opening and closing the gripper.

Figure 2. SimReady Central supplies the asset models and simulation settings and the example scene and controls define the pick-and-place task.

A robot can look visually correct while stationary in Isaac Sim but move or interact with objects incorrectly when the simulation runs. Before running pick-and-place, test its joints, movement, and contact behavior. You can ask the agent to perform these tests or do them manually in Isaac Sim.

During pick-and-place, watch whether a beverage can stay in the gripper as the arm moves. Asset structures vary, so use the settings in your loaded scene as your starting point. We will be going through the overall process of downloading the assets and composing the scene in the steps below.

This example combines the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can in Isaac Sim. The task is to grasp the can, lift it, move it to a target, and release it. You can also leverage SimReady Central Space search service endpoint to look for OEM curated content.

We will also use a frontier AI model to help create and run the task code in an open Isaac Sim scene. For this example, we use GPT-6 Sol, but another agent and model combination may work if it can load the required skills and execute Python against Isaac Sim (generated code and results can vary). The prompt provides a starting point. Inspect the generated code and check the resulting behavior before adapting the task.

Open SimReady Central and find the UR17G arm, Robotiq 2F-140 gripper, and beverage can used here. Select Download on each asset, then use Save to folder or the supplied Hugging Face command. Keep all three complete asset folders intact so Isaac Sim can find their supporting files.

Use the asset versions linked in this example and provide your agent with the local USD file paths for the arm, gripper, and beverage can. An example gripper path is shown below; your download location may differ.

Figure 3. SimReady Central search and interactive previews help identify the Robotiq 2F-140 gripper and beverage can used in this example.

Figure 4. The beverage can’s download options include saving the asset package to a folder or using the Hugging Face CLI.

The arm validation report uses the Robot-Body 4.0.0 profile and the gripper validation report uses Robot-Gripper 3.0.0. Both record passing PhysX driven-joint checks, which inspect joint-drive settings.

SimReady profile validation provides a shared baseline for reusing these assets. The pick-and-place run then tests how the arm, gripper, can, and controller work together in the assembled scene.

With the assets downloaded, use your agent with Isaac Sim skills to help assemble the robot, run validation tools, and create the pick-and-place controls. You can also perform these steps manually using the linked documentation.

Start Isaac Sim from its installation directory with the remote Python server enabled so the agent can interact with the simulation through Python:

If you are using an agent, make sure you start it from the Isaac Sim directory so that it can access the skills needed while going through the steps below.

Confirm that all three assets appear without missing-file errors. Ask the agent to inspect the arm and gripper’s joint limits and drive settings, or review them yourself in Isaac Sim. The robot and the gripper contain physics joints which can be tested and validated in the Isaac Sim GUI as well. We will now assemble the arm and the gripper next so that we can control the assembly as a single articulation.

You can follow the Robot Assembler tutorial for manual assembly. Here we will ask our agent to complete the assembly and validate it for us:

The agent ends up using the ‘isaac-sim-remote’ and ‘usd-articulation’ skills packaged with Isaac Sim to complete the assembly and validate the physics of the robot. We now have all the assets needed for running pick and place; the assembled robot and the soda can. We will now proceed with the final portion of the workflow.

Figure 5. Joint settings for the UR17G arm and Robotiq 2F-140 gripper in Isaac Sim.

#9962. How AI Agents Could Change Workplace Communication Forever

Co-founder of Hellomatik (https://hellomatik.com), Madrid.

Co-founder of Hellomatik (https://hellomatik.com), Madrid.

Co-founder of Hellomatik (https://hellomatik.com), Madrid.

The thing that costs us the most time inside a company is not the work. It is explaining the work to each other.

The way we communicate at work has changed many times: the letter, the memo, the meeting, email, group chats. The medium changed every time; the thing underneath it never did. And that thing is simple: being understood has always been the speaker’s job. Whoever sends the message picks the words, tries to be clear, and hopes they got it right. Whoever receives it takes what arrives and makes do.

That is about to flip. Communication, inside a company and between companies, will stop passing through people. Each of us will have an agent of our own, a digital copy of us, and those agents are the ones that will talk to each other. Something deeper than the medium changes with them. The work of being understood moves from the speaker to the listener, because each person receives the information in their own terms, the way they understand it. It reads strangely on paper, but I already work like this every day, and going back is hard.

I am not writing from the outside, and I am not neutral, which is why I can tell you what you gain, what you lose, and what should worry you.

There is a children’s game that explains the whole problem. One child whispers a sentence to the next, who whispers it to the next, and by the time it comes back it has turned into something else. The same thing happens in a company, except it costs money. You explain a task to a colleague on a call, and details are already lost there. He understands it through his own experience and his own department; if he has to pass it to a third person, he tells it his way; and what arrives at the end is a copy of a copy, filtered by someone who may have misread it. No one lied. Each step simply cost a little.

When a team rarely gets this wrong, we say they have good chemistry, and we treat it as a skill and an advantage. But chemistry is luck. Today the most valuable employee tends to be the one who takes in the most and passes it on best, the one who garbles the message least. All that skill exists to make up for a flaw in the channel. That flaw is about to disappear, and with it the need to depend on who carries a message best.

For this to work, each person will have their own agent inside their computer, a digital copy of them. We all know the kind of program that opens for one task, closes when it is done, and starts blank the next time. Your agent does not start blank. It keeps your way of working from one task to the next, like a colleague who has worked beside you for years. I call it your higher self, an idea I have written about before: you, but never starting from scratch.

I understand artificial intelligence as an equal to work with, not as a tool. The brain and the hands belong to the same body, and no one thinks of calling their own hand a tool. You bring the judgment, and your agent carries out what the two of you decided. It does not work for you, it works with you.

What makes that agent different is that it knows you: how you understand things, what you need in order to grasp something on the first try, how you write. That is the piece that makes it possible to turn communication around.

With an agent like that on each side, the message stops traveling the way it does in the game. When a matter has to pass through several colleagues, each one has an agent. The first, the one who meets the problem, works it through on its side. It clears up what is missing, asks the questions a person in a hurry would skip, and brings its own judgment to it. What it passes on is the full information, raw, with none of its own reading laid on top.

Then the receiver’s agent takes over. It does not hand the block across untouched. It reads it, orders it, and explains it to its person the way that person understands things. Some of us do best with an analogy, others with a plain description, others with a drawing. It seems like a detail, and it is the difference between getting something on the first try and not getting it at all. At that point the ground shifts, in a way that is hard to see at first: being understood stops being the speaker’s job and becomes the listener’s. Everyone receives the same thing, told to their own measure.

This might look like the game of telephone again, now between machines, where one completes and the other reinterprets. The difference is exactly what made the game unreliable. In the game the message shrank in every mouth, and no one could see where. Here the content travels whole and in writing. What changes from one side to the other is the form it takes, never the substance, and the judgment an agent adds fills in what is missing rather than trimming it to fit. Because all of it is on the record, you can always see what was said and where.

That same agent then shares the information out across the team by each person’s role. It never sends anyone what they are not meant to see, such as payroll, billing, or sales. The hierarchy holds, and the information reaches each person whole.

How many times have you sat in a meeting, been asked whether anyone had questions, and said nothing out of embarrassment? When the project reaches each person complete and explained in their own terms before they sit down, the meeting stops being the place where things get lost. Today that information is scattered across half a dozen places: cloud drives, messaging apps, email threads. Gathering it where one agent knows the whole task, and everything that came before it, changes the starting point. The work begins with someone who has already read all of it.

We already communicate this way. I tend to be the one who finds the opportunities and deals with the larger clients, so I get messages that the technical team has to handle, on things outside my area. Before, each of those messages meant a call or a meeting to explain what the client wanted. Now I explain nothing.

When one reaches me, my agent reads it in full, with all my inboxes in front of it, and instead of summarizing it writes the task with the context inside it: the emails, the threads, the attachments, what it has checked in the product, and how we will know it is done. The task arrives complete. It goes to a board and is assigned to whoever it belongs to by role. My colleague does not get my hurried version. He gets the whole situation, and his agent explains it to him the way he understands it. No one has lost half an hour on a call, and nothing has fallen through.

All of it stays in writing, tagged by client and in order, and anyone can pick it up again later. When the work is done, his agent tells mine, mine tells me we can move on, and it leaves me a draft reply to the client written the way I write, because each of us is, underneath, a bundle of rules, and I have taught mine to my agent.

This is not a program we open in order to work. It is how we talk to each other. And it is what I mean when I say a company’s communication will stop passing through people. We already do it here, every day.

The cost is belonging. The same optimization that improves the communication closes each person inside their own world. They work more apart from everyone else and talk more with their agent than with their colleagues. There is a great deal to gain, because everyone asks, flags, and explains with the whole context in front of them, nothing filtered, and none of it lost in a meeting. And something goes that was never part of any task: the conversation nobody needed that held people together, the moment colleagues understand one another without trying. It is what remote work brought, taken a step further, and it is better not to pretend it comes free.

It works for almost any job that runs on passing information around, which is nearly all of them apart from the purely manual ones. Communication is one of the biggest drains on time there is; some people spend the whole day in meetings. Many are necessary. Others would sort themselves out on the inside, between agents.

None of this stays inside the company. Today an email comes in from someone outside with an offer, and your agent reads it. In the same way we trade emails now, our agents will pass the information between them, and you will work through it with yours before you decide. Whoever accepts an offer does it with the whole context in front of them and can engage with what they were sent, rather than decide on the little they had time to read.

Many companies already do a version of this, in a crude and makeshift way: people copy and paste their emails into a chat so someone can tell them what is being asked. Once this becomes normal, there will be nothing to copy and paste. The agent will take in the full context of the documents, and you will receive it already shaped and explained, so that all you add is your judgment.

The first is data leaking out. Inside an organization it has to be absolutely clear that a person’s role decides what information they can receive, with strong guardrails at every step so that nothing ever crosses between levels. The second is intent leaking out: what an agent sends to someone outside can reveal an offer that was never meant to leave. For that, you have to think hard about who is on the receiving end and design the communication so that it stays safe without becoming stilted.

The risk that worries me most is not technical. If the agent reads the original and the person gets it already explained, there comes a point when nobody goes back to the source, and a mistake by the agent can travel without anyone catching it. The answer is not to trust that the agent will never slip, because it will. The answer is that the person stays where the decisions are made. You do not hand over the judgment, only the work of carrying the message. The agent prepares, orders, and proposes; the person signs the decision and the reply, which is why what reaches them is a draft and not a settled fact. Without that human part in the decisions, the whole thing comes apart. And because all of it is written down, a mistake can be found and traced, unlike the spoken message, which used to vanish without a mark.

I expect it to become the norm within the next decade, though we already work this way ourselves, with our higher self handling both the work and the running of it. The more people lean on artificial intelligence, and the less time they lose fighting with information that arrives half-complete, the sooner it comes. And how well colleagues work together will stop depending on whether they happen to click. It will be good whatever skills each of them has.

It is worth asking what all of this is for, past the time it saves. There is a consequence that answers it, and it is easy to miss. For as long as we have worked, the person who explained themselves best was worth more, because the channel was poor and someone had to make up for it. When the channel stops being poor, that advantage fades. What stays scarce is not carrying a message well but choosing well: the judgment to decide what is worth doing, the taste, the knack for making something matter.

That is where the time we now spend explaining ourselves goes. It does not vanish into the air; it comes back to the person, and what is left is not less work but different work. The mechanical part, carrying and translating the message, falls to your agent. The part that is only yours, the deciding, stays with you, and it fills the space that passing messages around used to take. Working this way does not make you less human. It moves the work from execution to intention, which is where a person’s work always had its worth.

One last question is left, and I will not answer it here. Will all of this carry over to the way people deal with one another outside of work? I will save that for another essay.

Originally published at isaac-correa.github.io. Earlier essays: The Death of Search and The Last Tool.

The End of the Mouse: How AI Could Change the Way We Use Computers

#9961. Hugging Face and OpenRouter join forces to make open-weight models easy to run

Hugging Face and OpenRouter are teaming up to make open-weight models easy to run. Every major open-weight release is already being published on the Hugging Face Hub, and OpenRouter serves those models at scale, routing each request across 80+ providers based on live measurements of each one. Together, every open-weight model on the Hub that a provider serves can be called with your Hugging Face token, through the same API, with the best provider picked for each request.

Today, we are switching Inference Providers from our own custom router to OpenRouter's. Requests made to language models now go through OpenRouter, which picks the best provider for each call based on live price, speed and reliability, and retries on another provider if the first one fails. Your code stays the same.

The router supports OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs and Anthropic's Messages API for every chat model, whatever the provider behind it. Pick your coding agent or SDK and a model, then copy the steps, or copy the whole setup as a prompt for your agent:

Setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi and Hermes Agent

The same Hugging Face token also gives you storage with Storage Buckets, compute with Jobs and dedicated inference with Inference Endpoints. PRO, Team and Enterprise plans include monthly credits for compute and inference.

On OpenRouter, open-weight models went from 26.8% of the tokens served in October 2025 to 71.7% at the end of September 2026, after peaking at 77.5% in July (OpenRouter, October 2026). Over the same period, weekly open-weight volume grew more than 60-fold, against almost tenfold for closed models. This week, the most used model on OpenRouter is an open-weight one, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, with 59.2 trillion tokens (rankings).

Open-weight models cost about four times less on average: $0.28 per million input tokens and $1.62 per million output tokens, against $1.27 and $6.36 for closed models.

The best open-weight models still trail the best proprietary ones on the hardest benchmarks. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, Kimi K3.1 Pro, the best open-weight model, scores 46 against 65 for Claude Fable 5.2, at about a seventh of the cost per task ($3.68 against $26.54). For a lot of workloads, that trade-off is worth it.

OpenRouter serves more than 800 trillion tokens a month to over 10 million users, across 600+ models from 80+ providers. Its routing is based on live measurements of every provider across that traffic.

OpenRouter recently rebuilt its provider routing: instead of only looking at the lowest list price, it sends each request to the provider with the best mix of price, speed and reliability.

When a provider slows down or starts failing, traffic moves away from it until it recovers, and a failed try is retried on the next best provider inside the same call. In OpenRouter's measurements, the new routing cut capacity errors by 46% and improved time to first token by 16.9% and throughput by 16.3%.

Before, Inference Providers picked one provider for your request and returned its error if it failed. Now, the request is retried on another provider. You can still choose a policy or a provider with a suffix on the model id:

Routing is also cache-aware: a conversation stays on the provider that holds its prompt cache. To make it explicit, send a stable UUID per conversation in the X-HF-Session-Id header (see the prompt caching guide).

Pricing doesn't change: you pay the provider's price on your Hugging Face bill, and Hugging Face doesn't add a markup on top of it. PRO users get $2 of credits every month, and Team and Enterprise organizations get $2 per seat. See Pricing and Billing for the details.

Image, video, and audio generation continue to work exactly as before, directly through Hugging Face Inference Providers without going through OpenRouter. You can keep using the same token and API, and access tens of thousands of LoRAs.

On model pages, you can chat with the model right away in the widget. Two new tabs show what's behind it: Providers lists every provider OpenRouter can route the model to, with its input and output price, speed and uptime over the last 24 hours, and Metrics shows the best price, throughput, time to first token, context length and uptime among them:

Your usage overview breaks your spend down by the provider each request went to:

In your settings, you can turn off any provider you don't want: the router never sends your requests there. Organizations have the same settings, and they apply to every request billed to the organization.

Requests to language models now go through OpenRouter and are billed to your Hugging Face account or organization, so you can no longer use your own API key for a provider with these models. You can still pick a provider with a suffix on the model id (model:provider) or turn providers off in your settings, and your code stays the same. Custom keys for image and video providers keep working.

This is the first step of our partnership with OpenRouter. Next:

Try a model, or read the Inference Providers docs to get started.

#9960. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

#9959. What the Microsoft 365 outage says about change risk

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

The Microsoft 365 outage on November 12 and 13 2026 knocked out Exchange Online, which sits behind Outlook, for about 24 hours. Microsoft Teams, SharePoint and other services were hit hard as well. Microsoft says it wasn't one mistake but rather a latent defect from a July fix, a routine Teams failover and nearly 14% of gateway capacity already out that all lined up at peak US traffic.

Press reports citing Microsoft's preliminary report show the disruption lasted from 4:20 PM UTC on November 12 to 4:10 PM UTC on November 13, and users in 74 countries and territories reported problems to Downdetector within about an hour.

Microsoft has said the outage was a technical issue and was not related to hackers, cyber activity, or to AI, and I'll take that at face value because it isn't what this post is about.

What caught my attention is how Microsoft describes the cause: not one mistake, but three ordinary things lining up.

In an abridged root cause posted on November 16, Microsoft's Charles Lamanna described three factors behind the failure of a networking gateway that fronts many Microsoft 365 services.

Together, the last two pushed the gateway into the latent bug during peak US traffic, and rerouting then sent load to the remaining servers until more than 80% were unresponsive at the worst point. Microsoft says bulkheads between partitions didn't stop the cascading failure, due to a separate issue it hasn't yet explained.

Normal load testing missed the defect because the test labs leaned toward weaker, lower-core hardware, and the contention gets worse on newer machines. Exchange Online couldn't fail out of the gateway the way other services could, and Microsoft's normal rollback and feature flags couldn't quickly revert a months-old change. Engineers wrote an update that returned the code path to its previous known-good state.

Look at each ingredient separately: a fix that passed staged deployment, a failover that Microsoft describes as normal, a capacity shortfall with enough headroom to absorb it, load tests built around weaker hardware, and rerouting that does what rerouting is supposed to do. Each one is routine, and in most large engineering organizations, each would sit with a different person or team, such as performance engineering, platform networking, service owners, operations or release engineering.

I don't know how Microsoft is organized, and I don't know whether anyone there had the full picture of the change risk, or whether the picture existed anywhere at all, which is an important distinction. Knowledge can be fragmented, meaning someone knew and it never reached the decision, or it can be missing, meaning nobody knew the problem existed. Shared context clearly helps with the first. It helps with the second only when joining existing records surfaces a contradiction, such as "production runs on hardware your tests don't cover."

In my experience, failures like this are hard to see from any individual seat, and they sit in the part of reliability that dashboards don't capture because the relevant knowledge isn't a metric. It's the relationship between a change, the environment it runs in, the state production is in today, and what happened the last time something similar broke.

The defect ran for more than three months without causing a problem, and it's tempting to read that as evidence the change was safe. But my read is that it shows something narrower: the conditions that trigger the bug hadn't happened yet.

Staged rollout was used here, so "roll out gradually" isn't the lesson: staging verifies the conditions that occur during the rollout, but it can't verify the ones that haven't occurred yet, like a failover landing on a gateway that is already 14% short during peak traffic.

Metrics like change failure rate have the same limit because they count failures that have already happened, and tests have it too. Tests encode assumptions, and assumptions go stale when the fleet or traffic mix changes, so a test suite that is green for a hundred days only says the assumptions held for a hundred days.

Engineering teams we talk to describe the same shape of problem regardless of scale. A software development director at an enterprise software company described what happens when experienced people leave:

"We're losing knowledge, I think, faster than we're gaining it."

An engineering practitioner at a mid-market software company described the gap between a developer's view and the whole system:

"They test it in their isolated environments. It goes into the large pre-production environment that has lots of changes flowing in. And we're kind of bottlenecked on like human review at this point."

Neither is describing Microsoft's failure, but both describe the same underlying condition: the knowledge needed to judge a production change, and assess the risk of that change, is spread across people, environments and history. Nobody holds all of that mission-critical knowledge when the decision is made.

Change risk assessment starts with an honest look at the upcoming change, the environment it will run in, and the state of production today. These five questions come from Microsoft’s account of the incident, but apply to any software team, and you can answer them without any new tool.

No tool guarantees prevention, and simulation is only as good as the context behind it. Testing, review, staged rollouts, and well-designed recovery are still required workflows.

What we've built is aimed at the gap those questions point to. PlayerZero builds an engineering world model from a company's code, tickets, telemetry and past incidents. It gives you a living map of how a system is connected and how it behaves in production. It captures the "why" behind earlier incidents and fixes, so precedent is something a team can query instead of something one senior engineer remembers.

On top of that, code simulations run a proposed change against how the system actually behaves, including dependencies across services and repositories, before it merges. The aim is to help a team ask better questions before a change ships: what else does this touch, and what has gone wrong near here before?

Cayuse's Chief Information and Technology Officer, John Nord, said that PlayerZero "has improved our ability to proactively detect and address issues earlier in the development lifecycle." Cayuse reports catching 90% of customer-facing issues before production and resolving issues 80% faster.

Generic LLMs and AI tools can help, but they don't have the kind of shared organizational context that is behind every response in PlayerZero.

#9958. Rumble-2-Flash: an open 0.5B speech model for 40+ languages

Today we're open sourcing Rumble-2-Flash under the Apache 2.0 license. It's a 0.5B-parameter speech recognition model for 40+ languages that competes with models 3-60x its size.

audio accepts a local path, a URL, a NumPy array, or a list of these.

Rumble-2-Flash uses the Qwen3-ASR architecture for day-0 support. If your stack runs Transformers or vLLM, it runs Rumble-2-Flash, with no forked runtime or trust_remote_code.

To find out how small a model could get before accuracy dropped off, we distilled Rumble-2, our larger production model, into it with on-policy distillation. The student doesn't train on transcripts the teacher wrote. It transcribes the audio itself, and the teacher grades that transcript token by token: at every position, it gives its own probability for what should come next, and the student learns to match it. Because the student learns from its own outputs, it gets corrected on exactly the mistakes it makes, with feedback on every token instead of one score per clip.

On-policy distillation normally requires teacher and student to share a tokenizer, and ours don't: choosing Qwen3-ASR meant taking its vocabulary too. GOLD removes that restriction. It merges tokens where the two tokenizers split the text differently, so both models are compared over the same text. Tokens that exist in both vocabularies are compared directly, and the rest by their sorted probabilities.

On the Open ASR Leaderboard multilingual track, Rumble-2-Flash averages a 6.96% error rate across Chinese, German, French, Italian, Spanish, Portuguese, Hindi, Dutch and English. That's better than Meta's omniASR-LLM 7B, a model 15x larger, and ahead of Whisper large-v3. On the English track it averages 6.6% WER.

Rumble-2-Flash is also fast. Its throughput depends on how full the batches are: on the larger datasets in HF's Open ASR Leaderboard, where batches stay full, it reaches over 7,000 RTFx. That's an hour of audio in about half a second.

Clean audio is easy. Phone calls are compressed and noisy, and often have speakers with very different accents. On AppTek's call-centre benchmark (302 hours of helpline calls, 14 English accents, scored with AppTek's own script), Rumble-2-Flash reaches 7.86% WER, on par with NVIDIA's Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe (30B) at 7.78%. That's well ahead of Qwen3-ASR 0.6B (8.7%), from the same model family, and close to Qwen3-ASR 1.7B (7.4%), the only model in the comparison that does better.

The weights are on the Hub at Reson8/Rumble-2-Flash. It's also available through our API.

We're very curious what you'll build with it. Tell us in the Discussions tab what you've made, what you like, and what you'd like to see changed in a next version.

#9957. What is high-extraction flour, exactly?  : A baker’s guide to our new T85 Baker's Reserve Bread Flour.

High-extraction flour is a technical term that often prompts a lot of confusion from those unfamiliar with it. But with the debut of our new high-extraction flour, known as Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour, we’re breaking down just what it is and why it's a great choice for avid bread makers.

The extraction rate of a flour refers to how much of the original grain — the bran, germ, and endosperm — ends up in the final flour. A high-extraction flour typically has an extraction rate of about 80% to 90%, meaning some of the bran and germ have been sifted out, but it still retains much of the original grain. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning its extraction rate is 85%.

To put that in perspective, whole wheat flour has an extraction rate of 100%; it retains the entirety of the grain, including the bran, germ, and endosperm.

High-extraction flour falls between white and whole wheat flour. It’s lighter and less coarse than whole wheat flour because some of the bran has been sifted out, but it still retains more flavor, nutrients, and color than white flour, since it retains much of the original grain.

High-extraction flour is popular for artisan bread baking because it offers a balance of nutrition and good gluten development. It’s great for rustic loaves, baguettes, and pizza dough, and particularly well-suited for sourdough baking because it strikes a balance between flavor, nutrition, fermentation, and dough strength.

You can substitute our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour 1:1 for bread flour (by weight or volume) in artisanal bread recipes; it can also be used 1:1 to replace the total flour in recipes that call for a combination of all-purpose and whole wheat flour. If you're subbing Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour for all-purpose flour in a bread recipe, you may find you need to add slightly more liquid to the recipe.

Bread bakers love high-extraction flour for artisan bread and sourdough because it offers the flavor and nutrition of whole grain flour; the stronger gluten development and more open crumb you get from white flour; and better fermentation from the minerals present in the bran and germ, which feed the wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria in sourdough starter, promoting more active fermentation.

If you want a loaf of bread that’s more flavorful and nutritious than bread made with exclusively white flour, but that still rises high and has an open crumb, high-extraction flour is a great choice.

Yes — in fact, it’s a great choice for feeding starter because of the sourdough-friendly minerals present in the flour, which boost activity in your starter.

Yes! T85 is a French specification that refers to the extraction rate (85%) of the flour. Our Baker’s Reserve Bread Flour is a T85 flour, meaning the extraction rate is 85%. If you have a recipe that calls for T85, this flour is the perfect choice.

#9956. 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers

Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation.

I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory.

Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk.

I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me.

My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi. That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim.

When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next.

Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090!

It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp, at 13.5 tok/s.

That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed.

Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token?

llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU (--cpu-moe, --n-cpu-moe N, -ot "exps=CPU", or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache (--moe-cache-mib) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits.

vLLM's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU.

Transformers offloads through Accelerate (device_map="auto", offload_folder), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward. For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing.

I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags:

Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s.

If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box.

Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work.

All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming.

I started with OLMoE-1B-7B, which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers.

First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm, which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel.

The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool: one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla.

I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained, in huggingface/transformers#50717. To try it, install Transformers from that PR:

Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next:

That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script: the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table.

Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout.

The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option.

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So:

The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping.

The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming, on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s.

Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts:

Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page.

I also tried vllm-metal, vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache.

Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped:

Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now:

These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts:

That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers.

Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it.

It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work.

Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader, and prebuilt kernels from the Hub. All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub, and the project loads them from there.

Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time.

The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717, and the benchmarks are in the Space. Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome.

Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM.

Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata. Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went.

A GGUF conversion of Tencent’s Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 draft model, intended for speculative decoding with a separate Qwen3.8-27B target model in a llama.cpp fork. It is not a standalone chat model. The maintainer is aj9o9.

Use it to accelerate Qwen3.8-27B generation, especially code, math, and tool-call workloads. The supplied RTX 3090 tests also show gains on mixed chat tasks, but prose and image-heavy requests may benefit less; tune draft length for your GPU and workload.

Requires both a compatible Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF and the dspine branch of the llama.cpp fork; stock llama.cpp does not load these files. Longer drafts consume more VRAM and reduce available context: on the tested 24 GB RTX 3090 setup, Q4_K_M with 15 drafted tokens fit up to context 65,536, versus 98,304 with 7 drafted tokens. Speculative decoding can produce different output from non-speculative runs, including at temperature 0. Performance figures are hardware-, backend-, prompt-, and setting-dependent; community results use differing test conditions.

On the tested RTX 3090, Q4_K_M DSpine at 15 drafted tokens reached 90.1 tok/s on a mixed short-context task set, compared with 51.7 tok/s for DFlash2 and 28.2 tok/s without speculation. Code and math were the strongest measured tasks; prose was slower than code and math. The same test setup reported maximum context of 65,536 for DSpine at 15 drafts, 98,304 for DFlash2 at 7 drafts, and 176,128 without speculation. These are results for the stated setup, not general rankings. Other GGUF alternatives listed in the supplied sources include Qwen3.8-27B-S-mirai-GGUF, Qwen-3.8-27B-ROCmFP4-FAST-GGUF, Qwen3.8-27B-i1-IQ4_KS_KT-GGUF, and Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF.

This is a five-layer speculative drafter that reads hidden states from five target-model layers and drafts a 16-token block in parallel. Its described mechanisms include causal block attention, a gated code bridge after each layer, and serial last-write refinement over candidate predecessor tokens. Available files are Q4_K_M (1.26 GB; code-bridge tensors remain BF16), Q8_0 (2.20 GB), and BF16 (4.06 GB, described as intended for re-quantizing). The files contain only the drafter. The supplied RTX 3090 benchmark used a Q4_K_M Qwen3.8-27B target, q8_0 KV caches, one slot, and the CUDA dspine branch. It measured 90.1 tok/s on a mixed task set at temperature 0; task-specific results were 128.7 tok/s for code, 122.8 for math, 62.0 for summarize/translate, and 41.6 for prose/story. These are reported measurements, not guarantees. The supplied abstract describes DSpine research results on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B in SGLang; it does not establish those results as measurements of this GGUF conversion or its Qwen3.8-27B use.

Use a compatible Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF together with one of the drafter GGUF files. The documented llama.cpp server setup accepts a target path (-m) and drafter path (-md), with controls including --spec-draft-n-max, context size (-c), slot count (-np), and optional probabilistic draft sampling. The README warns that auto-fit may not reserve enough memory for the drafter; set context size explicitly. On 24 GB cards, two slots with 15-token drafts do not fit according to the supplied guidance.

The drafter proposes token blocks for speculative verification by the target model; it does not independently provide final text generation. The decoder can select a draft chain greedily or by sampling. Output may differ from a run without a drafter because verification batches tokens and can change near-tied token choices; the source says code and tool calls usually match, while prose and image descriptions can diverge.

The example is the documented CUDA setup. Adjust --spec-draft-n-max and -c for your GPU and memory; the source recommends testing draft sizes such as 2, 3, 4, 7, and 15.

A: No. These files contain only the draft model; pair one with a Qwen3.8-27B target GGUF.

Q: Which quantization should I start with?

A: The README recommends Q4_K_M, whose code-bridge tensors remain BF16. Q8_0 is larger and uses more VRAM, while BF16 is described as a full-precision file for re-quantizing.

A: In the reported RTX 3090 setup with a Q4_K_M target and q8_0 KV cache, the maximum context was 65,536 with 15 drafted tokens and 98,304 with 7. Actual capacity depends on the setup.

Q: Does speculative decoding preserve identical output?

A: Not necessarily, even at temperature 0. Batched verification can change near-tied token choices; the source reports that code and tool calls usually match, while prose and image descriptions can diverge.

Q: What does the supplied research abstract establish?

A: It reports DSpine research results on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, including SGLang serving tests. It does not establish those figures as benchmarks for this Qwen3.8-27B GGUF conversion.

But when we do get the chance, we want a slam-dunk recipe — or 12. Here’s a dozen of the favorite fall recipes we’ll be making this month: from pumpkin cake bars to spooky fudge brownies to a crowd-pleasing vegetarian quiche.

It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown! Only this version comes in cake form. The decoration is deceptively easy: Stack two small Bundts, frost the entire thing, and add a chocolate-dipped ice cream cone for the stem.
