These bite-sized pies are a charming addition to any occasion. The boiled cider and spices in the filling ensure a full depth of apple flavor for maximum fall vibes. If you're tight on time, swap the lattice treatment for a buttery crumb topping instead.

Ready to test the theory that only white flour can make rolls light and fluffy? A bit of bread flour and vital wheat gluten give these whole wheat rolls a lofty rise, while the milk, butter, and honey create a plush crumb that stays soft for days. Add a salted honey butter wash to the tops of a freshly baked batch, and you may not have any leftover.

Get the recipe: Super-Soft Whole Wheat Rolls

If you like this recipe, you may also like: Whole Grain Dinner Rolls, Soft White Dinner Rolls

"Tassie" means "small cup" in Scottish, and these dainty pecan pies pack a nutty punch. The cream cheese pastry crust is cut into rounds and placed in a mini muffin pan before the pecan pie filling is spooned into each well. With only 30 minutes of hands-on time, these two dozen tassies come together quickly on a crisp fall afternoon.

#9952. Two Personality Traits Linked To A Sharper Mind

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

How you respond to beauty may have more in common with your thinking skills than you realise.

Intellectual curiosity and an appreciation of beauty are both linked to stronger thinking skills.

People with these qualities tend to perform better on tests of literacy, numeracy and problem-solving.

The findings suggest that a person’s interest in ideas and aesthetic experiences may offer clues to their cognitive abilities.

Curiosity could encourage people to seek out opportunities to learn, while stronger thinking skills could make exploring complex ideas more rewarding, with both processes reinforcing one another.

Intellectual curiosity involves enjoying ideas, wanting to understand things and being drawn to questions that require thought.

Aesthetic sensitivity describes an appreciation of art and beauty.

Both qualities belong to the broader personality trait of openness to experience, which captures how receptive people are to unfamiliar ideas and experiences.

However, openness also includes creative imagination, and this aspect showed no significant independent association with cognitive performance.

Imagination, curiosity and an appreciation of beauty may overlap in everyday life, but their relationships with thinking skills differ.

The conclusions come from an analysis of almost 68,000 people across 12 countries, including Canada, Germany, Italy and New Zealand.

They completed personality questionnaires alongside assessments of literacy, numeracy and the ability to solve problems as circumstances change.

Intellectual curiosity and aesthetic sensitivity were linked to better performance across all three assessments, even after accounting for other personality traits.

The connections between personality and cognitive skills also varied between countries.

Educational systems and cultural practices could help explain such differences, although the reasons remain uncertain.

Overall, the findings link both a desire to understand the world and an appreciation of its beauty with stronger thinking skills.

The study was published in the journal Large-scale Assessments in Education (Rammstedt et al., 2026).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9951. Time-Series Models in the Streamhouse: A New Frontier and Use Cases

Real-time forecasting, anomaly detection, and optimization, powered by IBM time-series models with more than 50 million downloads. Now available natively on Confluent, in the cloud and on premises, running on CPUs.

Every business generates a continuous record of change: a machine reading, a payment, a sale, an order, or a change in inventory. These observations form time series, and they carry signals that can help teams anticipate what happens next.

The challenge is turning those signals into decisions while they still matter. A forecast delivered after a production run, a stockout, or a payment authorization may be accurate, but too late to influence the outcome.

IBM and Confluent are bringing time-series foundation models closer to the data as it flows. With Apache Flink, teams can apply forecasting , anomaly detection and semantic intelligence to streaming data using SQL, making model outputs available to the applications and people responsible for the next action.

Foundation models have changed how organizations work with text, images, and documents. Time-series foundation models extend a similar idea to numerical data by learning general patterns from diverse historical data and then applying that knowledge to new series and tasks. The models can provide a starting point without requiring teams to train a separate model for every series. Depending on the task and deployment, teams can also fine-tune a model or combine its outputs with other data and business logic.

Figure 1. More than 50 million downloads, and the family of four models behind them

Now the time series foundation models run natively inside Confluent as built-in functions in the cloud and on premises. In Confluent Cloud they are fully managed, with nothing to deploy (documentation). On premises, the models can run within your own infrastructure using Confluent Platform for Apache Flink.(documentation). The models run on CPUs, without requiring GPUs.

The models can support a range of mission-critical use cases, from helping keep production lines in spec and detecting unusual store activity to improving product-level planning. They can also provide signals to assess card payments and forecast trading volume to help place large orders. These building blocks can be applied across manufacturing, retail, banking, and airlines, bringing insights closer to where decisions are made.

See how time series and real-time context come together to create value:

Businesses operate continuously. Orders are updated, payments arrive, shipments are delayed, and inventory changes throughout the day. Yet the information behind these events often sits across systems that update at different times or rely on periodic batch processes. When applications and AI agents act on outdated or inconsistent information, they risk making decisions that no longer reflect what is happening.

A Streamhouse addresses this by continuously capturing, processing, governing, and serving current business context. Confluent’s Data Streaming Platform brings together five capabilities—connect, stream, process, govern, and query—to make that context available to applications, analytics, and agents. Apache Flink transforms and enriches data as it flows, while Lightning Tables provide low-latency access to the current state.

Figure 2. The Streamhouse on Confluent: from existing data sources to current business context that agents, applications, analytics and lakehouses use anywhere.

Time-series models add predictive power to this architecture. Flink can prepare the data, invoke forecasting and anomaly detection, and make the results available alongside the events that produced them. Other models—including large language models, statistical models, and specialized machine learning systems—can contribute where appropriate.

Figure 3. The intelligence layer of the Streamhouse: time series models, large language models, and ML and statistical models, with orchestration across them.

This approach can help teams in four ways:

-Scale model development. A pretrained model can provide a common starting point across many time series, reducing the need to develop and maintain a separate model for each one.

-Refresh predictions as data changes. Forecasts can incorporate recent observations as part of a streaming workflow, subject to the model’s requirements and the pipeline’s configuration.

-Put signals closer to decisions. Forecasts and anomalies can be routed to operational applications sooner, where teams can combine them with business context, rules, and human judgment.

-Run compact models on CPUs. The models are small enough to run on standard CPUs alongside the streaming pipeline, in the cloud or on premises, which can reduce the need for dedicated GPU infrastructure and simplify deployment.

Figure 4. Stream native time-series intelligence on Confluent

The following scenarios illustrate how organizations could combine time-series models, streaming data, and application logic.

An ice cream line’s quality depends on overrun—the amount of air whipped into the mix. Today, the process engineer and operator rely on QA lab measurements taken after the tubs are filled. If a new cream lot or a warm, humid day changes the process, hours of production may already need rework by the time the team sees the result.

To get ahead of the problem, a pretrained TTM model reads SCADA telemetry and QA measurements every 10 minutes. It forecasts the share of tubs expected to be in spec four hours ahead, along with a likely range.

When the forecast falls below the plant’s target, an optimization process evaluates combinations of freezer draw temperature and airflow. Because the model takes these control variables as inputs, it can score each option before anything changes on the line. The operator approves the recommended setpoints, while routine adjustments can be automated within predefined guardrails.

The outcome is a more proactive process: less rework, lower energy use per tonne, and more consistent quality. The same approach can be applied to ovens, dryers, kilns, and mills.

Figure 5. A forecast of product quality helps the operator evaluate freezer setpoints before making an adjustment.

A store operations team monitors sales for thousands of products across hundreds of stores. Fixed thresholds often flag predictable weekend peaks while missing quieter changes, such as a product selling less than expected. As alerts accumulate, it becomes harder for the team to know where to focus.

AI_DETECT_ANOMALIES gives each sales series an expected range based on its recent history. Each new reading is compared with that range at a confidence level the team chooses, without training a separate model for every product and store.

When sales fall outside the expected range, the signal can be combined with inventory and store data to help identify a likely cause and recommend a next step—for example, checking the shelf or replenishing stock. The same approach can be applied to machine sensors, API telemetry, meter readings, and payment volumes.

Figure 6. Store sales are compared with an expected range. In the view shown, recurring peaks remain within the range and no anomaly is flagged.

A category planner and a replenishment team need to keep products available across every store without carrying excess inventory. But forecasts may be refreshed only once a week, often focusing on top-selling products, while the long tail is managed with simpler rules. When sales patterns change between planning cycles, one store can run out while another has too much stock.

With AI_FORECAST, a pretrained model can forecast demand across products and stores. In this example, it produces a 28-day forecast with a P10–P90 range, refreshed as new sales data arrives. The planning application combines the forecast with inventory, lead time, and the planner’s chosen service level to calculate a reorder point.

When stock is projected to fall below that point, an agent can draft a purchase order for review. The same approach can support planning for spare parts, staffing, ATM cash, and energy demand.

Figure 7. A store-level demand forecast informs a reorder point and a proposed purchase order for oat milk.

Fraud teams already rely on sophisticated rules and models to evaluate transactions. One continuing challenge is that a threshold applied across many cardholders may not reflect how each person normally spends.

A time-series signal can add that individual context. In this example, each payment is compared with an expected spending range based on the card’s recent history. A transaction outside that range is passed to the bank’s existing fraud systems as an additional input, alongside other signals and business rules.

The bank can then decide whether to approve the payment, request additional authentication, or investigate further. The decision and the signals behind it can be retained for review.

Figure 8.A payment outside the card’s expected spending range prompts a step-up authentication in an illustrative fraud workflow.

An execution desk needs to divide a large order into smaller trades while managing its effect on the market. Historical volume curves offer a starting point, but today’s trading activity may look very different from the average.

On each one-minute bar, PatchTST-FM forecasts trading volume for the next 30 minutes, with a P10–P90 range. The execution algorithm uses that forecast to pace the order within the participation limit set by the desk.

If a news event changes market activity, the algorithm can pause and replan. If trading is quieter than expected, it can reduce the size of each slice and signal that the order may take longer to complete. Each forecast and the resulting execution decisions can be retained in the audit trail.

Figure 9. Volume forecast informs the proposed execution schedule for a 100,000-share order.

A reliability engineer investigating an unusual sensor pattern may want to know whether similar behavior appeared elsewhere in the plant.

TSPulse can produce representations of time-series windows that support similarity search. In a separately built application, those representations could be indexed and used to retrieve historical patterns across equipment. An engineer could search for shapes such as a spike and recovery, a gradual rise, or a step change, then inspect the associated maintenance records and operating conditions.

This application requires an embedding pipeline, an index, and access to the relevant context. Similarity can help narrow an investigation; it does not establish a root cause by itself.

Figure 10. Time-series embeddings can support a search for similar patterns across equipment and other signals.

The same models and building blocks can support different workflows across industries:

Figure 11. The plant twin, from sensor to setpoint. A new cream lot pulls overrun off target. The forecast reads the line, the agent proposes a new draw temperature and air flow, the operator approves, and the tubs are back in spec. Simulated data.

Figure 12. The store twin, a store and its supply chain. A promo is coming for oat milk. The forecast prices in the promo and sets the reorder point, the agent raises a purchase order, the planner approves, and the shelf is full on promo day. Simulated data.

Banking: payments and the trading desk. The fraud lead wants to stop card testing without blocking good customers, and the trader wants a large order done without moving the price. Every card and every symbol is scored against its own expected pattern, event by event. Fraud and security holds the odd swipe before authorization, anomaly detection spots the unusual flow, and trading paces each order with the forecast volume.

Airlines: hub operations, fleet and network. Operations control wants to see a disruption coming while there is still time to act. Engine, gate and network streams are forecast and checked in real time. Anomaly detection catches the engine reading that drifts, production optimization rebalances gates and crews, and supply chain planning puts the spare part where the aircraft will be.

In every industry, the Streamhouse does the same work: Flink runs the Granite models to forecast, detect and optimize, Streaming Agents act on the live context, and people approve the exceptions.

Explore the models on Confluent to see how time-series intelligence can support real-time decisions.

#9950. Most Frequently Asked Questions About NFTs(Non-Fungible Tokens)

 


Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) are the most popular digital assets today, capturing the attention of cryptocurrency investors, whales and people from around the world. People find it amazing that some users spend thousands or millions of dollars on a single NFT-based image of a monkey or other token, but you can simply take a screenshot for free. So here we share some freuently asked question about NFTs.

1) What is an NFT?

NFT stands for non-fungible  token, which is a cryptographic token on a blockchain with unique identification codes that distinguish it from other tokens. NFTs are unique and not interchangeable, which means no two NFTs are the same. NFTs can be a unique artwork, GIF, Images, videos, Audio album. in-game items, collectibles etc.

2) What is Blockchain?

A blockchain is a distributed digital ledger that allows for the secure storage of data. By recording any kind of information—such as bank account transactions, the ownership of Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs), or Decentralized Finance (DeFi) smart contracts—in one place, and distributing it to many different computers, blockchains ensure that data can’t be manipulated without everyone in the system being aware.

3) What makes an NFT valuable?


The value of an NFT comes from its ability to be traded freely and securely on the blockchain, which is not possible with other current digital ownership solutionsThe NFT points to its location on the blockchain, but doesn’t necessarily contain the digital property. For example, if you replace one bitcoin with another, you will still have the same thing. If you buy a non-fungible item, such as a movie ticket, it is impossible to replace it with any other movie ticket because each ticket is unique to a specific time and place.

4) How do NFTs work?

One of the unique characteristics of non-fungible tokens (NFTs) is that they can be tokenised to create a digital certificate of ownership that can be bought, sold and traded on the blockchain. 

As with crypto-currency, records of who owns what are stored on a ledger that is maintained by thousands of computers around the world. These records can’t be forged because the whole system operates on an open-source network. 

NFTs also contain smart contracts—small computer programs that run on the blockchain—that give the artist, for example, a cut of any future sale of the token.

5) What’s the connection between NFTs and cryptocurrency?

Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) aren't cryptocurrencies, but they do use blockchain technology. Many NFTs are based on Ethereum, where the blockchain serves as a ledger for all the transactions related to said NFT and the properties it represents.5) How to make an NFT?

Anyone can create an NFT. All you need is a digital wallet, some ethereum tokens and a connection to an NFT marketplace where you’ll be able to upload and sell your creations

6) How to validate the authencity of an NFT?

When you purchase a stock in NFT, that purchase is recorded on the blockchain—the bitcoin ledger of transactions—and that entry acts as your proof of ownership.

7) How is an NFT valued? What are the most expensive NFTs?

The value of an NFT varies a lot based on the digital asset up for grabs. People use NFTs to trade and sell digital art, so when creating an NFT, you should consider the popularity of your digital artwork along with historical statistics.

In the year 2021, a digital artist called Pak created an artwork called The Merge. It was sold on the Nifty Gateway NFT market for $91.8 million.

8) Can NFTs be used as an investment?

Non-fungible tokens can be used in investment opportunities. One can purchase an NFT and resell it at a profit. Certain NFT marketplaces let sellers of NFTs keep a percentage of the profits from sales of the assets they create.

9) Will NFTs be the future of art and collectibles?

Many people want to buy NFTs because it lets them support the arts and own something cool from their favorite musicians, brands, and celebrities. NFTs also give artists an opportunity to program in continual royalties if someone buys their work. Galleries see this as a way to reach new buyers interested in art.

10) How do we buy an NFTs?

There are many places to buy digital assets, like opensea and their policies vary. On top shot, for instance, you sign up for a waitlist that can be thousands of people long. When a digital asset goes on sale, you are occasionally chosen to purchase it.

11) Can i mint NFT for free?

To mint an NFT token, you must pay some amount of gas fee to process the transaction on the Etherum blockchain, but you can mint your NFT on a different blockchain called Polygon to avoid paying gas fees. This option is available on OpenSea and this simply denotes that your NFT will only be able to trade using Polygon's blockchain and not Etherum's blockchain. Mintable allows you to mint NFTs for free without paying any gas fees.

12) Do i own an NFT if i screenshot it?

The answer is no. Non-Fungible Tokens are minted on the blockchain using cryptocurrencies such as Etherum, Solana, Polygon, and so on. Once a Non-Fungible Token is minted, the transaction is recorded on the blockchain and the contract or license is awarded to whoever has that Non-Fungible Token in their wallet.

12) Why are people investing so much in NFT?


 Non-fungible tokens have gained the hearts of people around the world, and they have given digital creators the recognition they deserve. One of the remarkable things about non-fungible tokens is that you can take a screenshot of one, but you don’t own it. This is because when a non-fungible token is created, then the transaction is stored on the blockchain, and the license or contract to hold such a token is awarded to the person owning the token in their digital wallet.

You can sell your work and creations by attaching a license to it on the blockchain, where its ownership can be transferred. This lets you get exposure without losing full ownership of your work. Some of the most successful projects include Cryptopunks, Bored Ape Yatch Club NFTs, SandBox, World of Women and so on. These NFT projects have gained popularity globally and are owned by celebrities and other successful entrepreneurs. Owning one of these NFTs gives you an automatic ticket to exclusive business meetings and life-changing connections.

Final Saying

That’s a wrap. Hope you guys found this article enlightening. I just answer some question with my limited knowledge about NFTs. If you have any questions or suggestions, feel free to drop them in the comment section below. Also I have a question for you, Is bitcoin an NFTs? let me know in The comment section below

#9949. AI Code Generation Is Only One Small Piece Of The ROI Equation

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

The short answer: To measure AI ROI in software engineering, look past how fast code gets written. Count the engineering hours your team spends after the code exists, on triage, diagnosis, prioritization, review, and release for escalated customer issues. Then estimate how much of that time AI could recover, and value it at a loaded engineering rate.

AI coding tools help engineers implement features and explore solutions faster. But faster code only gets teams partway to a positive return on AI. Teams still need to review, test, and release changes, then diagnose and resolve defects that reach customers.

That work depends on understanding how the code behaves in production, which customer configurations matter, and what previous failures revealed. When each team has to reconstruct the same production context, time saved in the editor gets spent again downstream.

A more complete way to measure AI ROI includes the effort required to verify, release, and support the software teams produce: the work of production engineering. Drawing on what we've seen with customers, we built an AI ROI calculator that estimates the capacity tied up in escalated customer work, and how much of it an engineering world model can recover by connecting the evidence teams need to cut redundant investigation and coordination. Together, they bring a broader opportunity into focus: preserving more of the gains from faster coding and making each resolution useful beyond the issue that prompted it.

Run the AI ROI calculator to estimate how much engineering capacity your team could recover.

Faster implementation gives teams room to test ideas, refine features, and respond to customers. Those gains become harder to realize when the surrounding workflow still depends on people rebuilding the same explanation.

DORA's 2026 report, The ROI of AI-assisted Software Development, emphasizes that faster coding doesn't automatically translate into business value. It identifies reducing unnecessary rework as a way to reclaim engineering capacity and increase output without expanding headcount.

For teams already investing in AI code generation, that opens another investment question: how much capacity could AI recover from the work triggered by production defects? Customer escalations still require investigation, fixes need prioritization, and corrective changes need verification before release. Those responsibilities create an opportunity to extend AI's value beyond producing code.

An escalated customer issue makes those dependencies visible. Support rebuilds the customer's history. Engineering traces the failure through code and runtime evidence. Product seeks a reliable account of its impact, while QA establishes the conditions the fix needs to satisfy. When those findings stay scattered across tickets and conversations, each handoff adds another round of explanation.

Much of this effort is easy to miss because it appears inside otherwise necessary work. Investigating a defect is necessary; reconstructing evidence that another team has already assembled adds avoidable effort. Reviewing a change is necessary; asking its author to recover the reasoning behind its scope adds more.

The loss extends beyond labor cost: slower resolutions, interrupted feature work, less time for prevention, and senior engineers diverted into repeated explanations. Recovering that capacity means addressing repeated work across the full production workflow, from the first customer report to a verified release.

PlayerZero's engineering world model connects code, production signals, customer tickets, and prior outcomes into a persistent context that teams and agents share. Support, engineering, product, and QA can work from the same evidence about how the system behaves and what previous investigations established.

Shared context helps work move between teams without losing intent or scope. A discovery in support becomes available to the people and agents responsible for diagnosis, prioritization, and validation, reducing the work each team repeats.

PlayerZero's AI ROI calculator puts a number on that question for teams already using AI coding tools. It estimates a practical portion of the opportunity: recoverable effort across escalated customer work and the cost equivalent of that capacity.

Assembling evidence and coordinating escalations

Less escalation overhead and fewer clarification requests

Reconstructing symptoms and prior investigative work

More engineering capacity for unresolved causes

Establishing customer impact, related requests, and priority

Faster, better-informed decisions about engineering work

Reacquiring the fix context and rebuilding validation scenarios

Less review rework, and more focused release validation

The calculator uses illustrative effort assumptions and a loaded engineering rate to estimate the capacity teams could redirect toward planned delivery and reliability. The cost equivalent values that time before platform costs, providing a starting point for weighing the investment. The four stages below illustrate the repeated work reflected in the estimate and where shared context can reduce it.

Support's contribution begins well before a backend engineer picks up a ticket. L1 support clarifies the report and responds to the customer; support engineers connect it to sessions, documentation, related tickets, and technical evidence.

When those sources are disconnected, preparing an escalation becomes an investigation in its own right. Customer follow-up stretches out while support coordinates the people who might have the answer.

Consider a hypothetical customer whose data export times out when they request a large dataset with a particular filter enabled. Smaller exports still succeed. A report that simply says "exports are broken" leaves engineering with substantial work to do before it can investigate the cause.

PlayerZero connects customer reports to the relevant code and runtime conditions. In this example, support can pass along the affected configuration, request traces, and findings about which exports succeed or fail. The engineering world model keeps those findings connected to the report, giving engineering a defined technical case and support evidence for customer updates.

The immediate gain is less effort to prepare and clarify the escalation. Across a busy support queue, this returns time to customer work and reduces the interruptions needed to make an engineering ticket actionable. That means support can keep customers informed without every update depending on a specialist engineer's availability.

Backend engineers contribute specialized judgment, but a fragmented escalation can consume their time before they reach the unresolved question. They inspect logs and traces, review code history, and test competing explanations. If support's findings or a previous investigation are missing, they also retrace work that the organization has already completed.

That effort interrupts feature development and concentrates investigations around engineers who remember the affected system. The cost includes both the investigation and the planned work waiting for those engineers to return.

For the export timeout scenario, agentic debugging uses connected runtime evidence and code history to point to a query changed in a recent release. The engineering world model incorporates support's findings into this investigation, alongside the relevant changes, failure conditions, and explanations already considered. A confirmed cause gives product managers and engineering leads a technical basis for prioritization. They still need to connect customer impact to technical scope before deciding what takes precedence over planned work.

When that evidence is disconnected, effort accumulates in reconciling related requests, agreeing on the immediate response, and explaining why it matters more than competing priorities.

Engineering begins implementation with both the technical findings and the reason for the chosen response. Carrying agreed priorities and scope into the work reduces coordination demands and the need for repeated scope discussions, helping the team protect planned delivery.

A prioritized fix still needs implementation, review, testing, and release. Reconstructing the intended outcome, affected configurations, and regression coverage delays release decisions and consumes capacity that could otherwise go toward evaluating the change itself.

Coding assistance can accelerate the query change in the export example. Those conditions guide review, code simulations, and regression testing. Simulations predict behavior without executing the code, helping the team focus tests on potential risks; testing establishes whether the change meets the intended outcome.

With less effort spent reconstructing validation requirements, reviewers and QA can concentrate on correctness and relevant coverage. Release decisions are better informed, with engineering time going toward verifying the fix rather than recovering why it was needed.

After release, the engineering world model keeps validation results and production observations connected to the original report, diagnosis, and scope decision. Support and SRE teams can see what the fix covered, whether the customer's export succeeded, and what remains unresolved. That completed record gives support a grounded closing explanation and preserves the evidence behind the resolution.

The engineering world model's value extends beyond the effort saved on the current issue. PlayerZero's shared organizational memory makes configuration findings, decisions, and their rationale available across teams, so lessons from one investigation can inform future work.

PlayerZero's approach to memory and learning captures useful findings from completed work and incorporates corrections as conditions change, keeping the organization's accumulated experience useful over time. Teams can build on those findings while checking them against current evidence, rather than reconstructing each investigation from scratch.

#9947. Why your fine-tuning job takes longer than the FLOPs say

Predicting end-to-end fine-tuning time on shared GPU clusters, from 272 production runs.

A preview of our upcoming paper, Predicting End-to-End Fine-Tuning Time for Generative Language Models. The full version will be on arXiv soon.

GPUs are among the most expensive and scarcest resources in AI today. Anyone running a shared cluster has to decide, every day, which jobs go on which GPUs and in what order. That plan is only as good as the estimate of how long each job will take. When a job finishes hours early, GPUs sit idle until the next one is dispatched. When it runs hours late, everything queued behind it slips, experiments wait and delivery dates move.

Better duration estimates turn this into planning instead of guesswork: what runs, when, and on how many GPUs, with less idle capacity in between. Yet the estimate most teams use is a back-of-the-envelope FLOP calculation. It says nine hours, and the job finishes the next afternoon.

We wanted to know how far off that math really is, and whether we could do better before a job is even dispatched. So we took 272 real supervised fine-tuning (SFT) jobs from our production pool of NVIDIA H200 GPUs, about 7,382 GPU-hours in total, and compared analytical estimates against learned predictors.

The short version: the usual FLOP-based estimate explains little of what we observed (R² = 0.31, MAE 12.41 h). A CatBoost regressor that only sees information available before dispatch reaches R² = 0.98, with a mean absolute error of 1.71 h and a median error of 0.51 h in 5-fold cross-validation. The gap comes from two things a closed-form estimate cannot do. The regressor sees more training-specific signals, such as evaluation cadence, checkpoint policy, per-GPU load and fine-tuning regime, and it learns the nonlinear interactions between them from past runs.

For a dense Transformer, training costs roughly 6·P·D floating-point operations, where P is the parameter count and D the number of training tokens. Divide that by what your GPUs can deliver and you get a training-loop time:

Here N_GPU is the number of GPUs, FLOPS_peak is the peak throughput of one GPU from its spec sheet, and MFU (Model FLOPs Utilization) is the fraction of that peak the training actually achieves. Real jobs never run at peak because of memory traffic, communication and kernel inefficiencies, so MFU typically sits somewhere between 30% and 60%, and the right value for a given job is not known in advance.

This is a good description of the optimization loop. A job is more than its loop, though. Before the first step there is environment setup, model download and loading, and tokenization. During training there are periodic evaluations and checkpoint uploads. At the end, the final model goes to object storage. On a multi-tenant cluster, all of it competes with other jobs for network and storage I/O.

These overheads depend on configuration, and they do not scale neatly with workload or GPU count. Two jobs with the same nominal compute can finish hours apart.

To keep the comparison fair, the FLOP baseline we test counts the scheduled evaluation tokens as well as the training tokens, and we sweep MFU over a wide range.

We treat end-to-end duration as a supervised regression problem. Given a feature vector built from the job configuration and model metadata, predict the wall-clock time between the moment the job gets its GPUs and the moment it is done. Queue time is excluded.

We compared Linear Regression, Ridge, XGBoost and CatBoost. Feature selection combined correlation filtering, mutual information and permutation importance across 18 candidate feature sets, followed by a grid search with MAE as the criterion. The final CatBoost model uses 24 features.

Distribution of end-to-end duration across the 272 runs. Mean 23.43 h, median 15.29 h.

All numbers come from stratified 5-fold cross-validation. The first four rows are analytical and involve no fitting.

No single MFU value fixes the FLOP baseline. We swept MFU from 0.25 to 0.65. The best setting, 30%, still leaves a mean error above 12 hours on jobs that last 23 hours on average.

A more detailed analytical model does not close the gap. As a second baseline we took Calculon (Isaev et al., SC '23), an analytical performance model for LLM training from prior work. It builds an explicit layer graph and accounts for compute, memory traffic and inter-device communication. We extended the public implementation to cover LoRA, grouped-query attention, fused attention, bfloat16 and SwiGLU. Its estimates still correspond to a median of only 11% of the observed wall-clock time. That says nothing against Calculon as a step-level tool, which is what it was designed for. It shows how much of a production job happens outside the optimization step.

Linear models help, and then stall. Ridge brings MAE down to 7.23 h. The relationship between configuration and duration is not well captured by a purely linear model.

Gradient boosting does the heavy lifting. CatBoost and XGBoost land within one standard deviation of each other on every metric. We carry CatBoost forward because it has the lowest mean error across the board.

CatBoost's feature importance concentrates in a handful of features. Model and workload variables are there, as expected, but so are evaluation and checkpoint variables. num_eval_data, the total number of samples processed in evaluation over the life of the job, ranks first, followed by num_trainable_params, batch_eval_size_percent, num_all_params and num_gpus*batch_train_percent, with num_params_saved close behind. SHAP values tell the same story: high evaluation volume consistently pushes the predicted time up, while trainable parameter count has a nonlinear effect that only becomes large for the biggest models.

Mean feature importance of the CatBoost model across folds (PredictionValuesChange).

Feature importance is not a causal claim. Still, the pattern lines up with how a job is actually spent. How often you evaluate, how large the evaluation set is and how many checkpoints you persist all shape the wall-clock time, alongside model and dataset scale. These are choices people often make by habit when writing a training config.

One caveat on reading the plots: larger GPU allocations show positive contributions to predicted time. In our data, bigger allocations go with bigger jobs, so num_gpus acts partly as a proxy for job scale. It does not mean adding GPUs makes a job slower.

Looking at all 272 out-of-fold predictions, the median absolute error is 0.51 h. 80% of predictions are within 2.20 h and 90% are within 4.31 h. Broken down by job duration:

Up to 60 hours, the median error stays at about one hour or less. The long tail is where the model struggles, and with only 13 runs above 60 hours we read that as a data limitation.

Out-of-fold absolute error against real duration, colored by duration range. Errors stay low up to 60 h and widen in the sparse tail.

More data should still help. On a fixed 20% holdout, MAE drops from 1.63 h to 1.50 h when going from 85% to 100% of the training partition, with no clear plateau.

In practice, the predictor gives a scheduler a duration it can plan around before a job starts: which jobs to run together, when GPUs will free up, and whether a run will finish in time for its deadline.

What does transfer is the method: overhead-aware features, multicollinearity-aware selection and the comparison protocol. The full paper will report the feature formulas, the selection procedure, the search spaces and the final hyperparameters in full, so the pipeline can be rebuilt on any execution-log dataset with a similar structure.

Next on our list: hardware-specific descriptors and validation on other GPU types, transfer learning for configurations with few observations, other training objectives, and more data on long runs.

The full paper is coming to arXiv soon. Follow the Dharma-AI organization on Hugging Face to be notified when it is out, and leave your questions in the comments below. We would like to hear how you estimate job duration on your own clusters.

#9946. DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency

Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B, RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles. We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0%. Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks.

The checkpoints are available under Apache 2.0:

The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window. The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings.

We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats.

After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000, you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client:

The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content, and its final answer in content. These settings follow the model card’s quickstart.

DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%.

Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings.

Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes.

We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI, starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set.

RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. The learning runs on our internal training backend, which is built for agent training: each step learns from a handful of very long sessions, some as long as 1M tokens, folded into multiple trajectories via harness summarization.

57% lower training cost. On this release, 37% of each GPU’s peak compute went into useful training work (model FLOPs utilization, or MFU) on our backend. The open-source trainer, built on Megatron, reached 16% on comparable runs. So the same training needs 57% less GPU time. The gain is even larger on mixture-of-experts models: 6.2× on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, and more than 10× on the roughly 300B-parameter GLM-5.3-Flash.

2× faster end to end. Counting the time the agent spends on its tasks, the release run trained on about 16,800 tokens per second across its 144 GPUs. The open-source trainer reached about 8,300 on the same GPUs.

Stable over weeks. The release run trained for weeks on 144 H200s, 63,000 GPU-hours in total. From the first step to the last, its speed and efficiency held steady.

Every training step of the DaisyRose-27B release run on 144 H200s, plotted against total training time. Dashed lines: the open-source trainer on comparable runs.

Every training attempt runs in a sandbox: a fresh copy of the task’s environment where the agent runs commands, edits files, and is then graded.

Our service is built on the open-source AgentENV project, to which we also contribute fixes. Between mid-September and mid-November, it ran about 944,000 sandboxes for this project, with up to 1,566 running concurrently.

The service grew from one machine to as many as 12. We shipped ten upgrades to it, nearly all while training was running. Across all nine weeks, 99% of sandbox creations succeeded; since late October, that figure has exceeded 99.95%.

Cloud infrastructure costs for the project’s sandboxes were about 80% lower than running the same sandboxes with popular cloud sandbox providers. One way we keep costs down is to let each sandbox’s memory allocation grow and shrink with its actual usage, allowing more sandboxes to share each machine.

Download DaisyRose-27B, follow the SGLang serving guide, or use Miles to train your own agents.

We’d like to hear how DaisyRose-27B performs on your tasks, including where it falls short. Share your setup and results in the model’s Community tab.

We thank Eigent AI for working closely with us on training data, and the Qwen team for creating Qwen3.8-27B. We also thank the Miles and SGLang communities, along with other open-source projects including slime, AgentENV, and Harbor.

Adapted from the original RadixArk article.

#9945. Human in the Loop AI: How to Safely Scale Agentic Workloads with Tunable Autonomy

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Human-in-the-loop AI keeps people in charge of key decisions, while tunable autonomy lets teams expand what AI agents handle on their own as trust grows.

Most organizations experimenting with agentic AI run into two barriers long before they reach meaningful automation: the trust gap and the accountability gap. While teams trust AI enough to summarize tickets and recommend fixes, they don't yet trust it to investigate incidents or implement code changes on its own. And even when AI performs well, this doesn't transfer responsibility. Someone still needs to own the decision and be ready to reverse it if it goes sideways.

In mature engineering environments, both concerns are justified. Large codebases, shared infrastructure, customer commitments, and compliance requirements make it risky to let AI move from recommendation to autonomous action without oversight.

That’s why the answer is not full autonomy or full human control—it’s tunable autonomy that you can adjust as you progress in your AI adoption. With this operating model, organizations progressively expand what AI can do as trust grows, all while keeping a clear human owner at critical stages and full control over automated workflows.

Most teams begin with simple AI workflows, like summarizing incidents, explaining code changes, and drafting pull requests. The results are fast, and the downside is low—if the summary is wrong, a human catches it before anything breaks.

Those early wins create pressure to automate more. Leaders begin asking whether AI can take on higher-stakes work, such as classifying incidents, preparing fixes, and closing tickets.

That is where adoption stalls. That's why human-in-the-loop design matters.

Not all AI decisions carry the same weight. The same AI action that’s safe in one workflow can be dangerous in another. Auto-closing a duplicate support ticket carries almost no risk. Auto-deploying a production fix carries enormous risk. The action looks similar, but the consequences aren't.

And a single bad action is recoverable. What's harder to reverse is an agent that executes multiple steps on the same incorrect assumption. Consider an agent that prepares the wrong remediation plan. From there, it validates the wrong outcome and closes the wrong ticket. A small mistake turns into a cascading failure that grows harder to reverse.

The solution isn't to abandon AI altogether. The real leverage comes from building deliberate stopping points into the workflow. These checkpoints create a moment for human review before a mistake propagates, and establish a clear owner for the work that crosses that threshold. Over time, those approvals become the evidence base for every decision that advances AI's role.

The question, then, becomes how to place these checkpoints deliberately—and how to know when you have earned enough trust to remove one.

That is the problem tunable autonomy is designed to solve.

Tunable autonomy gives teams explicit control over how much AI agents can do at each stage of a specific workflow. Rather than making a one-time choice between full human control and full autonomy, organizations can set autonomy levels tailored to each workflow stage.

For each stage, they choose from the four levels:

The following table shows where most organizations start, and where each stage can realistically go.

Different workflows should progress at different speeds, and organizations should tune autonomy by repository, service, severity, ticket type, or team.

Setting AI autonomy levels within a team is relatively straightforward. Things get much more complicated when work crosses a team boundary. That's where introducing AI autonomy gates—checkpoints that determine whether AI-driven work can advance to the next stage or domain—matters most.

The reason is simple—each team has different standards, conventions, risk tolerances, and implicit knowledge, so they see the same issue differently. Support sees customer impact, engineering sees code paths, and QA sees reproduction risk.

Say an AI agent is classifying incoming support tickets. The agent’s actions stay within a single team’s domain, so the risk of a misstep is low and contained. When approval rates for AI-driven classifications trend near 100%, that workflow becomes a strong candidate for autonomous operation within your defined guardrails.

Now, say an AI-assisted workflow crosses a team boundary, like an AI-diagnosed issue moving from support to engineering with a recommended fix attached. The stakes rise because the fix comes with root-cause assumptions baked in—if one is wrong, it can travel through diagnosis, remediation, and closure before anyone with the right context catches it. And since engineering has to act on work they didn't produce, accountability for the outcomes becomes ambiguous.

That's exactly where an autonomy gate belongs. The gate ensures the work has been reviewed by someone who can vouch for it before it crosses that line. Each successful handoff, reviewed and acted on without issue, is how AI earns the next level of trust to take on more work.

To implement the tunable autonomy model across your organization, start by establishing full human-in-the-loop approval at every critical stage.

Even in recommend-only mode, AI creates immediate value for engineering teams. Connecting tickets to code, telemetry, and runtime behavior compresses investigation time to minutes. Surfacing likely root causes and recommending fixes streamlines resolutions, increasing customer satisfaction. Drafting pull requests and incident summaries keeps engineers focused on building.

Your team stays in the loop at every step, reviewing and course-correcting before anything moves forward. When their approvals reach close to 100% across workflows, gradually increase autonomy based on the following factors.

When you’re scaling AI workflows, you’re not just asking “Can the AI do this task?” but “Can it do it reliably enough to justify less oversight?” Metrics provide the most objective answer to this question.

Most engineering organizations already track these metrics for delivery performance and incident management. What changes with AI is what they reveal. Each one now also measures a different dimension of AI’s reliability.

Think of it less like flipping a switch and more like a new hire earning the right to make decisions without running them by a manager. Nobody hands over full autonomy on day one. It's granted incrementally by demonstrating sound judgment, catching mistakes before they compound, and building a track record that speaks for itself.

Autonomy can't advance without the professional judgment to back it. Approval from experienced team members ensures AI systems perform well across both familiar conditions and edge cases that only emerge under pressure.

Teams that get autonomy expansion right exercise their judgment across the dimensions where AI has the most influence and the least visibility: people, process, and context. They follow the same three questions before extending AI’s responsibilities further.

While metrics show that trust is building, satisfying these criteria tells you whether it's actually earned. When AI understands enough about your systems, your people, and your processes, it changes how work flows across the organization, increasing resilience and shifting defect resolution from reactive to proactive.

A helpful mental model is to apply the same bar you’d use for a senior engineer. Instead of micromanaging them, you trust that they've internalized the business context, know how handoffs work, and can navigate team processes without a checklist. An AI agent has to earn that same confidence, and teams need to build the evidence that it has.

Key Data’s experience is a blueprint for what it looks like when people, process, and context align with the metrics. By connecting customer-reported issues to the exact code changes and runtime behavior behind them, they eliminated the ambiguity that makes teams hesitant to rely on AI. With that context and the ability to reproduce and diagnose problems in minutes instead of weeks, the confidence to go further with AI across their workflow followed naturally.

Safe autonomy depends on strong controls—not just as a brake on what AI can do, but as the foundation that makes expanding its responsibilities possible. Despite differences in scale, stack, and risk tolerance, what those controls actually require tends to look the same across organizations.

The most trustworthy AI systems converge on four properties.

While these properties create a foundational audit system that keeps autonomy from becoming a liability, they're not sufficient on their own. Certain actions carry significant organizational weight, making human review essential regardless of how well the AI has been performing.

In these situations, the cost of getting autonomy wrong outweighs the efficiency gains from skipping the review. That’s why a checkpoint there almost always pays for itself.

The point isn’t to eliminate risk—it’s to make it manageable. AI agents will make mistakes, but they’ll make fewer than their human counterparts. With those controls in place, you can scale or decrease autonomy across teams while keeping errors contained and accountability clear.

At Cyrano Video, the combination of richer context and stronger trust allowed support teams to resolve more issues independently. As a result, the company reduced engineering time spent on support and bug fixes by roughly 80% while preventing many tickets from escalating in the first place.

Tunable autonomy only works when AI has access to the full engineering context—but in most organizations, that context is scattered across systems that don't talk to each other, leaving AI to act on an incomplete picture.

PlayerZero creates that visibility by unifying these signals into an engineering world model: a single representation of the system that connects intent, impact, real-world behavior, and institutional knowledge.

That foundation gives AI agents everything they need to meet the three conditions that teams use to validate readiness for higher autonomy: deep business understanding, clear visibility into ownership and escalation paths, and a reliable picture of process execution.

Cayuse shows what this model unlocks in practice. Using PlayerZero, they gave teams earlier visibility into issues and stronger confidence in the accuracy of AI-driven investigations. As a result, they found and fixed 90% of issues before users noticed and cut average resolution time by 80%.

Most organizations treat autonomy as a destination. The ones that scale it successfully treat it as a practice—something earned through evidence, refined through metrics, and extended only when trust is real.

That shift in mindset is what separates teams that adopt agentic AI from teams that build a lasting advantage with it.

PlayerZero is built for organizations that want to move fast with AI—without outrunning their ability to control it—giving teams the foundation to extend autonomy safely and the evidence to know when to go further. Book a demo to learn how.
