#9941. Introducing harness adapters: adapt your favorite model to your harness to improve performance and cost

Combining RL on a custom task distribution with your favorite agent harness yields more accurate and efficient models for that target harness and task distribution.

Models are not fully optimized for all harnesses and the tasks you’re doing. Instead, they target general performance. So when you combine a model and harness, you’re leaving performance and efficiency on the table for the stuff you’re actually doing. With RL, you can train a custom harness adapter that squeezes everything out of your model for your harness and task combination.

Take Qwen3.8-27B, its Terminal-Bench 2.1 score with the pi harness is 39% which uses on average 2.9K tokens per task. If we freeze those weights and add a custom RL-trained LoRA adapter we can get 55% pass@1, with average token usage of 1.5K. Most of this is down to the model reasoning less, calling less tools, and performing better first time.

Our earlier work (multi-harness RL, harness adapters) showed that RL on your own task distribution, inside your own harness, gives a more accurate and more efficient model. Those experiments covered data-analysis and code-building tasks. Here we wanted to push this further by exploring whether the result holds at 27B, on harder real-world software engineering tasks, across three harnesses: Pi, OpenCode and Hermes Agent. And most of all, share a fully reusable recipe, so you can reproduce this on your own task, harness, model combinations.

We leverage the Harbor integration in OpenEnv and TRL’s OpenEnv guide to train the model inside the harnesses we chose for the final training. We have built ready-to-use docker images for all our RL tasks that come with the target harnesses already pre-installed inside. In our final docker images, we use Pi 1.5.2, OpenCode 2.2.7 and Hermes Agent v0.22.6. The diagram below from the aforementioned blogpost explains well the entire protocol:

Most RL frameworks train a re-implementation of the agent loop: the agent is written against the framework's own interface, such as verl's AgentLoop, SkyRL-Gym environments, rLLM's agent and environment classes, slime's custom rollout functions, or ART's client inside your own Python agent. Here the harness runs exactly as it ships, and the trainer learns from the exact tokens it produced, recorded by a proxy between the harness and vLLM. Recent work moves in the same direction: Agent Lightning v1.0 keeps the deploy-time harness in the loop through a proxy ("harnessed agentic RL"), and SkyRL's Harbor integration trains on Harbor trials, converting their chat histories into tokens for the trainer.

For this recipe we created a custom dataset for agentic coding with the Hub, OpenEnv, and Repo2RLEnv. We combined together task retrieval of existing RL envs, task generation with Repo2RLEnv, task validation with OpenEnv, and sampling into a single data pipeline. This gave us the highest quality set of validated and relevant tasks to improve Qwen3.8-27B on agentic coding. In this section, we’ll walk through how we built it, so you can try it out on your own domains.

RL training needs tasks the agent can attempt, a verifier that scores each attempt, and evidence that the verifier is right. A verifier that accepts wrong answers teaches the wrong behavior. A task that is already feasible will not teach the model anything.

This section describes how we built the task set from three sources: two on the Hugging Face Hub and a third generated with Tasksmith, a pipeline in Repo2RLEnv. Every task passes an eligibility screen with openenv validate, and the same difficulty check against the base model, Qwen3.8-27B.

Each task uses the Harbor format, which Terminal-Bench 2.1 also uses. A broad search of the Hub for Harbor environments returned about 59,000 tasks, but they included duplicates, evaluation sets and tasks marked as not for training. We filtered down to just two Hub sources built for training and generated a third set ourselves:

We used Tasksmith to target gaps. We mapped the skills that our target benchmarks test (Terminal-Bench 2.1, the hard subset of SWE-bench Pro, and DeepSWE), then chose pull requests that exercise them, such as HTTP streaming, filesystem operations and serialization. From 30 merged pull requests, Tasksmith produced 24 tasks in 10 Python repositories that passed its checks, 17 of them on a second run. Its checks do not replace ours, so these tasks go through the same pipeline as the rest.

A metadata screen runs first. It keeps tasks from training splits with permissive licenses. It drops duplicates, tasks marked as not for training, the 253 tasks in our target benchmarks, and any task from a repository those benchmarks use. We then ran the semantic checks from openenv validate on every task in fresh trials:

Each trial ran as its own Hugging Face Job, which let us validate dozens of tasks at once. openenv validate offers the same option for any Harbor task:

858 of 1,127 Hub candidates passed. Wrong-answer controls caught defects, including a Tasksmith task that accepted an incomplete implementation and a Terminal-Bench 2.1 verifier (regex-log) that accepted known-wrong answers. Most failures were infrastructure problems, such as images that did not start. Failed tasks stay in a rejected split with the failing check recorded.

A valid task can still teach nothing. GRPO (group relative policy optimization) scores each attempt against the other attempts at the same task, so a task where every attempt passes, or every attempt fails, gives no learning signal. Before training, Qwen3.8-27B attempted each task 4 times, or 8 times for a stratified sample of six tasks per repository.

Of 442 scored tasks, Qwen3.8-27B solved 151 every time and 120 never. The 171 tasks it solved only sometimes form the qualified set. The figure below shows how the scores pile up at both ends and how they differ by source. The model solves most Go tasks every time, fails every attempt on more than a third of the SWE-smith Python tasks, and lands in the middle on 73% of the SWE-Gym tasks.

Qwen3.8-27B results on 442 scored tasks. Green marks the qualified tasks, which the model solves on some attempts but not all.

This example shows how we filtered and validated 1,127 tasks to 278 which we included directly in the final dataset. The pipeline then took the remaining 522 rejected tasks, repaired and complexified them with Tasksmith and repeated validation.

The pipeline applies two filters: validation removes broken tasks, and the difficulty check keeps tasks the base model solves only sometimes. This section tests whether those filters change what the model learns. We trained four short runs of up to 50 steps, each on tasks from a different stage of the pipeline, and compared them with the base model on Terminal-Bench 2.1.

Each run trains Qwen3.8-27B with LoRA and GRPO, using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer, on 32 tasks. All four use the same agent harness (OpenCode with up to 48 model calls), the same settings and one 8×H200 Hugging Face Job, and the reward is the verifier's pass or fail. The task sets differ in how they were filtered:

The figure below shows how the tasks impacted model learning. The table lists each run's steps and the checkpoint we evaluate. The chart tracks training reward across subsets of tasks with differing validation status.

harness-hub/agentic-coding-envs holds 871 tasks from 35 repositories. Hub tasks are capped at 40 per repository, so no single project dominates. The table below shows what each source contributes. The dataset has two views: every accepted task, and the qualified subset for GRPO training. Rejected attempts stay in a separate config.

We leveraged the stable version of AsyncGRPOTrainer from TRL, with the main advantage of the trainer being that it does not wait until all rollouts are completed before moving to the next training optimization step.

For more detailed reading on the trainer and its building blocks, please refer to the AsyncGRPO blogpost.

To obtain our final harness adapters, we trained LoRA adapters on top of Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B using TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer. The adapters were attached to the model using the all-linear flag. To maximize the training efficiency, thinking mode was turned off during rollout stages, and we evaluated our final adapter with and without thinking for broader comparison.

The final reward function consists of the verifier's correctness, combined with a small tool-efficiency bonus (0.1, derived from early experiments from the previous iteration of harness adapters which showed that 0.1 worked best).

We performed a small LR sweep on 50 steps using Termgrade environments (1e-5, 5e-5 and 1e-4) and noticed that 1e-5 barely moved training correctness (from 0.52 to 0.50), 1e-4 collapsed the rollouts instead of improving them (turns per rollout moved from 18 to 6, with entropy rising), and only 5e-5 clearly improved (from 0.49 to 0.60 by step 40). Longer 5e-5 runs then showed signs of instability (collapsing rollout lengths, rising entropy), so we settled on 2e-5 for the final runs.

Each harness adapter was trained using NVIDIA 2xB200 GPUs, with one GPU allocated for the vLLM server and the other allocated for the training process. We first performed some stress testing to maximize the amount of RL tasks that can be trained within a single optimization step. For that, we ‘maxed out’ the --token-budget argument from AsyncGRPOTrainer to its limit for the setup that we had. The chart below shows the evolution of the number of groups per step for each harness (in blue: Pi, green: OpenCode and orange: Hermes).

As the model gets better and better during training, it is able to fit more and more groups during each training step, which diversifies the signals that the model gets at each optimization step.

The final data mixture consists of 750 tasks from harness-adapters RL environments and 300 tasks from termgrade. In order to maximize the diversity of the sampled tasks during training, we have slightly customized the data sampling strategy, which will be explained below:

Before training, the tasks are put in a fixed order that interleaves them by family (i.e., their repository for our generated RL environments. For Termgrade, we just sorted them by name since each task is considered as its own family), so every training step mixes as many repositories as possible while following the distribution of the mixture.

We also plug the safeagents tool, in order to block any misbehavior from the model during training. The final plugin (which consists of the regex and pattern rules specific to the RL tasks and test path) is hosted in harness-hub/qwen-safeagents-plugin and can be used out of the box using the latest version of safeagents in case anyone wants to reproduce the training setup.

The number of blocked tools from safeagents decreases consistently during training, which indicates that the model gets ‘safer and safer’ after each optimization step. Below is a diagram of the safeagents blocked calls per 1000 tool calls, by training step, for each harness adapter.

Merging models often combines their capabilities while keeping most of what each one could do. Once the three harness adapters were trained, we asked two questions. Does merging them cost accuracy? And can a single "super-adapter" be accurate and efficient under every harness?

We started by comparing the weight updates of the three adapters, layer by layer. The cosine similarity between any two of them is about 0.01–0.02: each adapter pushed the model in a nearly orthogonal direction during training. That's the best case for merging, since the updates barely interfere.

We concatenate the three LoRA adapters along the rank dimension (PEFT's combination_type="cat"). The merged adapter has rank 96 (3 × 32) and applies exactly w · (ΔW_pi + ΔW_hermes + ΔW_opencode). Prior work on merging (task arithmetic, TIES, KnOTS) finds that scaling each update below 1 works best, so we compared three weights on all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks, under each harness, with the step-120 adapters:

The plain sum over-applies the updates. The agents become very short (13 tool calls per task, against 49 for the base model), and while Hermes peaks at 62.8%, pi falls back to the base model's level. The average dilutes each harness's own update. ½ gives the best balance, so we built the final super-adapter from the released checkpoints (pi step 160, hermes step 160, opencode step 150) at weight ½.

Under each harness, on the tasks every run graded (50–51 on SWE-bench Pro, 82–85 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), one attempt per task (in parentheses, the efficiency gain with respect to the base model):

"Thinking" is the chat template's thinking mode at its default effort (xhigh). The specialists were trained and served with thinking off.

With thinking off, the super-adapter improves on the base model on all six harness–benchmark pairs (mean pass@1 39.5% → 49.0%; 71 tasks newly solved vs 34 lost, p < 0.001).

Despite not being trained at all with thinking on, it's the strongest model we evaluated with thinking mode. Against the base model thinking at the same effort, it wins on five of six pairs and ties the sixth (mean 55.5% → 63.5%; 67 newly solved vs 37 lost, p = 0.004). The largest gains are on SWE-bench Pro: +16 points under hermes and +20 under opencode. Under pi on SWE-bench Pro, where thinking alone already reaches 74%, it ties.

Use the specialist harness adapters when thinking off. Each harness's own adapter is ahead on four of six pairs, by the most under pi (64.0% vs 46.0% on SWE-bench Pro, 56.5% vs 48.2% on Terminal-Bench). Splitting one model across three harnesses costs pi the most of its gain. If you only use one harness and keep thinking off, take its specialist.

The super adapter is also much more efficient. On the tasks both the base model and the super-adapter solve, with thinking off, it makes 53–73% fewer tool calls and generates 44–60% fewer tokens per task, with fewer tool calls on 111 of 130 tasks. With thinking on, it still cuts tool calls by 31–48% and tokens by 24–43% on SWE-bench Pro. On Terminal-Bench, tool calls drop by 19–25% and token counts stay about the same.

The ½ weight was chosen on Terminal-Bench 2.1 with the step-120 adapters, so the Terminal-Bench numbers are slightly optimistic; SWE-bench Pro played no part in the choice. Full paired results are in the super-adapter's model card.

This section reports what happened during training, then how the adapters score on held-out benchmarks inside and outside their own harnesses.

Training ran for a cumulative total of 598 steps, with a total of 78,114 samples trained, which consists exactly of 167M trained tokens.

During training, we see a clear signal that the model learns to solve tasks in fewer and fewer steps, with no clear sign of saturation. Despite having some clear increasing trend sometimes, training correctness seems to overall stay flat. This can be explained by the fact that the model meets new tasks during training, but the number of groups that fit in a step’s token budget more than doubles as trajectories get shorter. The accuracy gains show up on the held-out benchmarks in the section below.

On the other hand, safeagents was able to block multiple suspicious attempts. Across the three training runs, a total of 1.3M tool calls have been checked, and a total of 647 tool calls have been blocked.

This section covers the evaluation setup, the in-harness results, transfer across harnesses, and an out-of-distribution check.

We evaluate each adapter inside the harness it was trained in, on two agentic coding benchmarks: all 89 tasks of Terminal-Bench 2.1 (1 hour and 100 agent steps per task) and the 51 hardest tasks of SWE-bench Pro (2 hours and 100 agent steps). We cap the maximum number of tokens per task to be 131072. We do not tune the agent settings and use the default setup for all harnesses. For example, Pi does not keep previous reasoning turns while OpenCode and Hermes do, which mainly affects the SWE-bench Pro results due to rapid context overflow. Therefore you cannot compare the results across different harnesses (using Pi does not necessarily lead to better results than Hermes or OpenCode), but it is fair to compare results within the same harness and draw conclusions.

Every rollout runs through the same Harbor and OpenEnv stack as training, in HF sandboxes, with one attempt per task at temperature 0.8 and thinking off. Each LoRA checkpoint is merged into the base weights and served alone with vLLM on a single GPU, at the same concurrency as the base model's eval.

For all the evaluation benchmarks, we report the pass@1 as well as the number of tool calls, total turns, for all tasks and for solved tasks.

For openness, all model trajectories for final evaluations are pushed in this public bucket: harness-hub/harness-adapters-trajectories.

All three specialist adapters beat the base model under their own harness, on both benchmarks. On SWE-bench Pro (hard 51), pi goes from 39.2% to 64.7% (+25.5 points: 15 tasks newly solved vs 2 lost, p = 0.002), hermes from 29.4% to 43.1%, and opencode from 35.3% to 51.0%. On the full Terminal-Bench 2.1, pi gains +16.3 points (16 vs 2, p = 0.001) and hermes +14.1 (19 vs 7, p = 0.03). Opencode gains +6.0 overall, and +13.6 on the 66 tasks that played no part in choosing its checkpoint (12 vs 3, p = 0.035).

The adapters also solve tasks much more efficiently: on the tasks both they and the base model solve, they make 56–72% fewer tool calls per task on SWE-bench Pro and 53–70% fewer on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The single super-adapter beats the base model under all three harnesses too (+6 to +18 points on SWE-bench Pro, +5 to +10 on Terminal-Bench 2.1), with just as large a cut in tool calls (53–73%). It keeps less of each specialist's gain with thinking off, most under pi, but with thinking on it beats the base model thinking at the same effort on five of six harness–benchmark pairs (see the super-adapter section). Each model card has the full paired results.

To answer this question, we also evaluated the pi harness adapter under Hermes Agent and OpenCode.

Under OpenCode it matches OpenCode's own specialist on Terminal-Bench 2.1 (44.8% → 54.0%, against 46.4% → 52.4%). Under Hermes it keeps about two-thirds of the specialist's gain (46.3% → 56.1%, against 44.7% → 58.8%), with the same ~45% cut in tool calls in both. Therefore it seems that the newly learned capabilities are transferred across harnesses.

What happens if we evaluate in out-of-distribution tasks, outside the harnesses the adapters have been trained with?

We ran all five models on 300 AutomationBench tasks which consists of business-automation workflows evaluations, with AutomationBench's own agent loop instead of Pi, Hermes or OpenCode. This way, we can cross check two different questions: can the model solve problems outside SWE-related tasks? What happens when the model is being put outside the harness it has been trained with?

Results show that the adapters stay close to the base model. Pi and OpenCode are slightly ahead (27.0% and 25.3% pass@1 against 23.0%), the merged adapter is level (23.7%), and Hermes is a few points behind (17.7%). The differences are within noise, except perhaps Hermes, therefore RL inside the harnesses neither transfers clearly to this very different setting nor breaks the model on it.

We appreciate the feedback from the users and the community, initial testing and results from the community seemed overall extremely positive, and we wish to continue in this direction in the future. We also saw some surprising results, such as users reporting that the harness adapters work really well under Qwen3.8 derivatives, such as Swift-1.5.

This question is an open question we thought about, post-release. After inspecting carefully the generated trajectories from the evaluation benchmarks, it turns out the model, under non-thinking mode, tends to generate some short text before proposing a tool call, as opposed to the base model which generates the tool calls barely without any text beforehand.

This phenomenon can be seen as a sort of ‘reasoning leakage’, where the model learns to ‘escape’ from its non-thinking version to its thinking version by generating some text that can sometimes look like reasoning traces (e.g.: ..wait? ..let me see, etc.). A recent paper also describes behavior from LLMs during the RL stage very well.

Does this invalidate our models? We do not think so, as the final results are still valid; under the exact same conditions (fixed token budget) our adapters do outperform the base non-thinking model (by far) and match the performance of the thinking version, while being much more token efficient. This has been further confirmed by the positive feedback from the community.

However this raises the need of a proper follow up work, where we will try to re-apply the same pipeline for pure thinking models, as well as exploring hybrid thinking / non-thinking training, to better understand the behavior of RL training on hybrid thinking models. We will share with the community our next findings (and harness adapters), once we get conclusive results.

Throughout this work, we demonstrated that RL training your model inside your target harness leads to more efficient and therefore more accurate final models, when evaluated under the same conditions. This observation is in line and in continuation with several previous work from Hugging Face teams, such as multi-harness-RL or the early iterations of harness adapters.

In the future, we will explore applying this recipe to more models, while better studying the training strategies for hybrid thinking / non-thinking models.

We also share to the community openly the full recipe and pipeline to reproduce everything, and invite everyone to build their own RL tasks, derived from their own codebase, or any relevant materials, and apply the same training recipe and ideas to their favorite model and harness for more efficient agentic models. We hope this blogpost will serve as a starting point for builders to build and share their own harness adapters in the future.

Train open models with RL inside real agent harnesses

#9939. Speaking Faster Can Make You More Persuasive — Until This Happens

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Your best argument may lose its edge if listeners struggle to keep up with how quickly you deliver it.

Speaking at a lively pace can make a strong argument more convincing, but rushing can weaken its impact.

Very fast speech makes it harder for listeners to weigh up what they hear, reducing the advantage that good reasons have over weak ones.

The findings suggest that persuading someone depends partly on giving them enough opportunity to think.

The conclusions come from six experiments involving almost 4,000 people who listened to persuasive messages delivered at different speeds.

Across the experiments, increasing the pace from very slow speech initially improved impressions of the speaker’s confidence and encouraged closer consideration of the message.

However, these benefits eventually weakened or reversed as the delivery became faster.

This helps explain why simply telling someone to speak more quickly is incomplete advice.

A faster delivery can make an argument easier to engage with until the listener begins struggling to keep up.

Crucially, the consequences depend on whether the reasons being offered stand up to scrutiny.

In the two main experiments, listeners heard a proposal that would allow university students to pay lower tuition fees in exchange for working part-time.

Some heard strong arguments emphasising benefits such as smaller classes and better services.

Others heard weak arguments that included reduced leisure time and superficial improvements to the campus.

The recordings were digitally altered to change speaking speed while keeping other vocal features, such as pitch and intonation, unchanged.

Participants then rated their support for the proposal, with some also recording the thoughts that had occurred to them while listening.

The combined results showed that strong arguments gained an increasing advantage over weak ones as speech became faster, but lost some of that advantage at higher speeds.

In other words, delivery affected how effectively listeners distinguished a convincing case from an unconvincing one.

A central part of persuasion is how carefully people consider the reasons they are given.

When listeners examine a message closely, they have more opportunity to recognise its strengths, spot its weaknesses and form their own reactions.

This benefits a strong argument, while exposing the shortcomings of a weak one.

Very fast delivery can interfere with that process, making the merits of the message less influential.

The analyses suggested that changes in how easily listeners felt they could follow the reasoning helped explain this pattern.

Although speaking speed also affected how confident the speaker sounded, confidence alone did not adequately explain the overall pattern.

One possible reason very slow speech is less effective is that it makes sustaining attention more demanding, while excessively fast speech leaves too little time to absorb the content.

The experiments tested seven speaking speeds, ranging from 113 to 218 words per minute, but did not establish one ideal pace.

The most effective delivery is likely to depend on factors including the complexity of the message, the audience and the presence of distractions.

The findings also concern recorded persuasive messages, so they do not establish a universal rule for every conversation or public speech.

For someone presenting a strong case, the findings suggest keeping the delivery lively while giving listeners time to follow the reasoning.

Rushing may reduce the very scrutiny that would otherwise make a good argument convincing.

The study was published in the Journal of Nonverbal Behavior (Guyer et al., 2025).

Psychologist, Jeremy Dean, PhD is the founder and author of PsyBlog. He holds a doctorate in psychology from University College London and two other advanced degrees in psychology. He has been writing about scientific research on PsyBlog since 2004. View all posts by Dr Jeremy Dean

#9938. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features

Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.

To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.

When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows).

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab.

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts.

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9937. Borrowed UI: Why Your Next Desktop Tool Might Just Need a Browser Tab

I build developer tools. Go, React, SQL, and opinions with a commit history.

I build developer tools. Go, React, SQL, and opinions with a commit history.

I build developer tools. Go, React, SQL, and opinions with a commit history.

A local tool needs a table, a few charts, and some buttons. Somewhere in the planning meeting, it acquires an entire desktop application.

Before that happens, I want to nominate the browser already sitting on the machine.

I call this Borrowed UI, or BUI: a local process does the work, and a browser tab provides the interface. The established name is a local web UI. The architecture is old. I’m just giving my enthusiasm an acronym.

pprof is the cleanest example. It can print a report of expensive functions, or open a local web interface when a visual inspection helps. Same profiling data, another way to look at it. A graph does not have to become a whole desktop product.

With pprof installed and an existing profile file, its web mode looks like this:

Graph visualizations can require Graphviz. This is an example of an optional interface, not a promise of zero dependencies. pprof documentation.

Syncthing is the background-service version. Its browser GUI lets you inspect and configure synchronization. The GUI and REST API share a port, normally on loopback. The work belongs to a running process; you visit the control panel when you need it. Syncthing’s GUI documentation.

Jupyter is the richer version. The browser edits the notebook, while a server and execution kernel handle the other side. Close the tab and the kernel can keep running. Reopen the notebook and reconnect. Useful separation—and a reminder that “I closed it” needs a precise meaning. Jupyter Notebook documentation.

Jupyter is not a tiny installation. It illustrates the boundary, not a diet plan.

I’d consider BUI for a local data explorer, profiler, backup monitor, or service configuration tool. Especially when the useful part already works as a CLI or background process and the interface is something you need occasionally.

Browsers are good at tables, text selection, charts, responsive layouts, and accessible controls when we build them properly. The local process can own validation, credentials, durable state, and cancellation. The tab doesn’t need a second interpretation of the rules.

This also avoids distributing a browser engine with every application. It does not make the browser’s memory or CPU use disappear. Somebody still pays the rendering bill.

If your product depends on native menus, global shortcuts, file associations, or a carefully controlled window lifecycle, a native app or system WebView may be a better fit. If the whole interaction is one command and three lines of output, opening a tab is probably a small ceremony nobody requested.

You also inherit browser compatibility, port conflicts, startup and reconnection work. Closing the tab and stopping the process are different actions. Say so. Offline use needs local assets and capabilities; localhost is not an offline strategy by itself.

And localhost is not a security policy. Bind to loopback by default, validate Host and Origin, protect state-changing requests, and deliberately secure any wider network exposure. Syncthing’s documentation explicitly calls for authentication and HTTPS when exposing its GUI beyond the local machine.

I don’t think every desktop app should become a tab. I think this option deserves a place in the initial discussion. When a tool mostly needs to work quietly and occasionally explain itself, the browser is a pretty good place for that explanation.

This essay revisits ideas from my earlier BUI article with different examples.

#9936. How long can butter sit out?: For the best baking success, here's the deal on saving softened butter for later.

The bakers of King Arthur are here to solve the kitchen conundrums you share with us, whether it’s on the phone, computer, or by the good old postal service. In Ask the Baker’s Hotline, Annabelle will pick the brains of the talented King Arthur Baker’s Hotline team to tackle some of your most-asked questions.

Ryan from our Baker’s Hotline is here with the answer.

You sure can! It will still work the next time you want to bake. But remember, as with any dairy product, there are always precautions to take.

The USDA recommends keeping butter at room temperature for no more than two days to prevent spoilage. Salt is a preservative and can lengthen the shelf life, but for the sake of this article, we’re talking about unsalted butter. (It’s more appropriate for baking and is the type called for in most King Arthur recipes.)

“If the butter has only been on the counter at room temperature for a few hours or overnight and has maintained a temperature below 70°F, it should be just fine to place back in the fridge,” says Ryan. “You may not notice a difference in the performance of the butter when you eventually use it, other than the wrapper being a bit wet or soft. Food safety-wise, it’s still good to use.”

“If the butter became very soft or started to melt during its time on the counter (or in the microwave if you were speeding up the process), you can put it back in the fridge, but it may not be the best to use in your recipe,” Ryan suggests. “You may notice when it solidifies that it’s separated or grainy. The water, fats, and solids in butter are an emulsion, which can break when melted and re-solidified.” If your recipe depends on butter to create air or structure, like a cake that calls for creaming butter and sugar, you’ll want to start over with new butter.

“If you used that butter in a recipe requiring creaming, the air you incorporate wouldn’t be as stable since the structure of the butter has changed,” Ryan says. “Your baked goods may not rise properly, and frostings may be soft and loose. Is it still safe to use? Food safety-wise, yes. But structure-wise, perhaps not.”

That butter can still be used for other things though! Extra-softened or even melted and re-solidified butter will still work perfectly to spread on toast or pancakes, to be made into brown butter, or to remelt and use in recipes calling for melted butter like a Graham Cracker Crust.

If your butter has been unrefrigerated for more than two days, you run the risk of it going rancid. As Ryan says, “There is no coming back from rancid butter.” It has a distinctly unpleasant flavor and a noticeable rancid smell that carries over into baked goods. It’s best to dispose of the butter if this happens.

But what if you want to keep your butter at room temperature for days at a time to slather on your morning toast? Ryan recommends storing your butter in a butter keeper if you want to leave it on the counter. “The water in the base of the jar creates an airtight seal, helping prevent the butter from spoiling. So long as it is stored away from direct heat and light, the butter in a container like this will be fine for a few days. Be sure to replace the water often and clean the container before filling again.”

“When working with butter in a recipe, I like to bring out and soften only the amount that is needed for what I am working on. That way, I don’t end up with extra butter that won’t be used right away,” he says. “Repeatedly moving butter from the fridge to the counter and then back invites spoilage and poor performance.”

In a rush? To soften your butter more quickly, Ryan advises, “Cut your butter into pats and place them on a plate in a single layer at room temperature. More surface area means that the butter will soften a bit faster!”

#9933. Ahrefs vs SEMrush: Which SEO Tool Should You Use?


SEMrush and Ahrefs are among the most popular tools in the SEO industry. Both companies have been in business for years and have thousands of customers per month.

If you're a professional SEO or trying to do digital marketing on your own, at some point you'll likely consider using a tool to help with your efforts. Ahrefs and SEMrush are two names that will likely appear on your shortlist.

In this guide, I'm going to help you learn more about these SEO tools and how to choose the one that's best for your purposes.

What is SEMrush?


SEMrush is a popular SEO tool with a wide range of features—it's the leading competitor research service for online marketers. SEMrush's SEO Keyword Magic tool offers over 20 billion Google-approved keywords, which are constantly updated and it's the largest keyword database.

The program was developed in 2007 as SeoQuake is a small Firefox extension

Features

  • Most accurate keyword data: Accurate keyword search volume data is crucial for SEO and PPC campaigns by allowing you to identify what keywords are most likely to bring in big sales from ad clicks. SEMrush constantly updates its databases and provides the most accurate data.
  • Largest Keyword database: SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool now features 20-billion keywords, providing marketers and SEO professionals the largest database of keywords.

  • All SEMrush users receive daily ranking data, mobile volume information, and the option to buy additional keywords by default with no additional payment or add-ons needed
  • Most accurate position tracking tool: This tool provides all subscribers with basic tracking capabilities, making it suitable for SEO professionals. Plus, the Position Tracking tool provides local-level data to everyone who uses the tool.
  • SEO Data Management: SEMrush makes managing your online data easy by allowing you to create visually appealing custom PDF reports, including Branded and White Label reports, report scheduling, and integration with GA, GMB, and GSC.
  • Toxic link monitoring and penalty recovery: With SEMrush, you can make a detailed analysis of toxic backlinks, toxic scores, toxic markers, and outreach to those sites.
  • Content Optimization and Creation Tools: SEMrush offers content optimization and creation tools that let you create SEO-friendly content. Some features include the SEO Writing Assistant, On-Page SEO Check, er/SEO Content Template, Content Audit, Post Tracking, Brand Monitoring.

Ahrefs



Ahrefs is a leading SEO platform that offers a set of tools to grow your search traffic, research your competitors, and monitor your niche. The company was founded in 2010, and it has become a popular choice among SEO tools. Ahrefs has a keyword index of over 10.3 billion keywords and offers accurate and extensive backlink data updated every 15-30 minutes and it is the world's most extensive backlink index database.

Features

  • Backlink alerts data and new keywords: Get an alert when your site is linked to or discussed in blogs, forums, comments, or when new keywords are added to a blog posting about you.
  • Intuitive interface: The intuitive design of the widget helps you see the overall health of your website and search engine ranking at a glance.
  • Site Explorer: The Site Explorer will give you an in-depth look at your site's search traffic.
  • Domain Comparison
  • Reports with charts and graphs
  • JavaScript rendering and a site audit can identify SEO issues.
  • A question explorer that provides well-crafted topic suggestions

Direct Comparisons: Ahrefs vs SEMrush

Now that you know a little more about each tool, let's take a look at how they compare. I'll analyze each tool to see how they differ in interfaces, keyword research resources, rank tracking, and competitor analysis.

User Interface

Ahrefs and SEMrush both offer comprehensive information and quick metrics regarding your website's SEO performance. However, Ahrefs takes a bit more of a hands-on approach to getting your account fully set up, whereas SEMrush's simpler dashboard can give you access to the data you need quickly.

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the elements found on each dashboard and highlight the ease with which you can complete tasks.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs dashboard is less cluttered than that of SEMrush, and its primary menu is at the very top of the page, with a search bar designed only for entering URLs.

Additional features of the Ahrefs platform include:

  • You can see analytics from the dashboard, including search engine rankings to domain ratings, referring domains, and backlink
  • Jumping from one tool to another is easy. You can use the Keyword Explorer to find a keyword to target and then directly track your ranking with one click.
  • The website offers a tooltip helper tool that allows you to hover your mouse over something that isn't clear and get an in-depth explanation.

SEMRUSH



When you log into the SEMrush Tool, you will find four main modules. These include information about your domains, organic keyword analysis, ad keyword, and site traffic.

You'll also find some other options like

  • A search bar allows you to enter a domain, keyword, or anything else you wish to explore.
  • A menu on the left side of the page provides quick links to relevant information, including marketing insights, projects, keyword analytics, and more.
  • The customer support resources located directly within the dashboard can be used to communicate with the support team or to learn about other resources such as webinars and blogs.
  • Detailed descriptions of every resource offered. This detail is beneficial for new marketers, who are just starting.

WHO WINS?

Both Ahrefs and SEMrush have user-friendly dashboards, but Ahrefs is less cluttered and easier to navigate. On the other hand, SEMrush offers dozens of extra tools, including access to customer support resources.

When deciding on which dashboard to use, consider what you value in the user interface, and test out both.

Rank Tracking

If you're looking to track your website's search engine ranking, rank tracking features can help. You can also use them to monitor your competitors.

Let's take a look at Ahrefs vs. SEMrush to see which tool does a better job.

Ahrefs



The Ahrefs Rank Tracker is simpler to use. Just type in the domain name and keywords you want to analyze, and it spits out a report showing you the search engine results page (SERP) ranking for each keyword you enter.

Rank Tracker looks at the ranking performance of keywords and compares them with the top rankings for those keywords. Ahrefs also offers:

You'll see metrics that help you understand your visibility, traffic, average position, and keyword difficulty.

It gives you an idea of whether a keyword would be profitable to target or not.

SEMRUSH



SEMRush offers a tool called Position Tracking. This tool is a project tool—you must set it up as a new project. Below are a few of the most popular features of the SEMrush Position Tracking tool:

All subscribers are given regular data updates and mobile search rankings upon subscribing

The platform provides opportunities to track several SERP features, including Local tracking.

Intuitive reports allow you to track statistics for the pages on your website, as well as the keywords used in those pages.

Identify pages that may be competing with each other using the Cannibalization report.

WHO WINS?

Ahrefs is a more user-friendly option. It takes seconds to enter a domain name and keywords. From there, you can quickly decide whether to proceed with that keyword or figure out how to rank better for other keywords.

SEMrush allows you to check your mobile rankings and ranking updates daily, which is something Ahrefs does not offer. SEMrush also offers social media rankings, a tool you won't find within the Ahrefs platform. Both are good which one do you like let me know in the comment.

Keyword Research

Keyword research is closely related to rank tracking, but it's used for deciding which keywords you plan on using for future content rather than those you use now.

When it comes to SEO, keyword research is the most important thing to consider when comparing the two platforms.

AHREFS



The Ahrefs Keyword Explorer provides you with thousands of keyword ideas and filters search results based on the chosen search engine.

Ahrefs supports several features, including:

  • It can search multiple keywords in a single search and analyze them together. At SEMrush, you also have this feature in Keyword Overview.
  • Ahrefs has a variety of keywords for different search engines, including Google, YouTube, Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, and other search engines.
  • When you click on a keyword, you can see its search volume and keyword difficulty, but also other keywords related to it, which you didn't use.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush's Keyword Magic Tool has over 20 billion keywords for Google. You can type in any keyword you want, and a list of suggested keywords will appear.

The Keyword Magic Tool also lets you to:

  • Show performance metrics by keyword
  • Search results are based on both broad and exact keyword matches.
  • Show data like search volume, trends, keyword difficulty, and CPC.
  • Show the first 100 Google search results for any keyword.
  • Identify SERP Features and Questions related to each keyword
  • SEMrush has released a new Keyword Gap Tool that uncovers potentially useful keyword opportunities for you, including both paid and organic keywords.

WHO WINS?

Both of these tools offer keyword research features and allow users to break down complicated tasks into something that can be understood by beginners and advanced users alike.

If you're interested in keyword suggestions, SEMrush appears to have more keyword suggestions than Ahrefs does. It also continues to add new features, like the Keyword Gap tool and SERP Questions recommendations.

Competitor Analysis

Both platforms offer competitor analysis tools, eliminating the need to come up with keywords off the top of your head. Each tool is useful for finding keywords that will be useful for your competition so you know they will be valuable to you.

AHREFS



Ahrefs' domain comparison tool lets you compare up to five websites (your website and four competitors) side-by-side.it also shows you how your site is ranked against others with metrics such as backlinks, domain ratings, and more.

Use the Competing Domains section to see a list of your most direct competitors, and explore how many keywords matches your competitors have.

To find more information about your competitor, you can look at the Site Explorer and Content Explorer tools and type in their URL instead of yours.

SEMRUSH



SEMrush provides a variety of insights into your competitors' marketing tactics. The platform enables you to research your competitors effectively. It also offers several resources for competitor analysis including:

Traffic Analytics helps you identify where your audience comes from, how they engage with your site, what devices visitors use to view your site, and how your audiences overlap with other websites.

SEMrush's Organic Research examines your website's major competitors and shows their organic search rankings, keywords they are ranking for, and even if they are ranking for any (SERP) features and more.

The Market Explorer search field allows you to type in a domain and lists websites or articles similar to what you entered. Market Explorer also allows users to perform in-depth data analytics on These companies and markets.

WHO WINS?

SEMrush wins here because it has more tools dedicated to competitor analysis than Ahrefs. However, Ahrefs offers a lot of functionality in this area, too. It takes a combination of both tools to gain an advantage over your competition.

Pricing

Ahrefs

  • Lite Monthly: $99/month
  • Standard Monthly: $179/month
  • Annually Lite: $990/year
  • Annually Standard: $1790/year

SEMRUSH

  • Pro Plan: $119.95/month
  • Guru Plan:$229.95/month
  • Business Plan: $449.95/month

Which SEO tool should you choose for digital marketing?

When it comes to keyword data research, you will become confused about which one to choose.

Consider choosing Ahrefs if you

  • Like friendly and clean interface
  • Searching for simple keyword suggestions

  • Want to get more keywords for different search engines like Amazon, Bing, Yahoo, Yandex, Baidu, and more

 

Consider SEMrush if you:

  • Want more marketing and SEO features
  • Need competitor analysis tool
  • Need to keep your backlinks profile clean
  • Looking for more keyword suggestions for Google

Both tools are great. Choose the one which meets your requirements and if you have any experience using either Ahrefs or SEMrush let me know in the comment section which works well for you.

#9932. A Patch Assurance Workflow for LiteLLM Gateways

CVE-2026-40217 is a LiteLLM guardrail sandbox escape that allowed command execution in the proxy process. The endpoint required administrator or master-key authentication in the default configuration, and the default Docker image ran the service as root. CISA added the vulnerability to KEV on 2026-11-18. CVE.org records CVSS 3.1 score 8.8, while the GitHub advisory records CVSS 4.0 score 7.5.

A gateway patch has several dependencies: package version, container digest, endpoint routing, administrative identity, secrets, and network placement. A useful assurance workflow keeps those dependencies visible from planning through closure.

The custom-code test endpoint filtered submitted Python at the source level. X41 showed that string construction and bytecode rewriting could bypass the checks and recover real builtins through a sandbox function. The attacker could then import os and run commands with the proxy's permissions.

The attack required an affected version, a reachable endpoint, and an administrative credential. A patch program should verify all three rather than assuming that one control proves the others. The KEV record provides urgency, but local evidence must establish actual exposure and remediation.

The proxy can hold provider keys and service credentials, route application traffic, and make policy decisions. Code execution can expose those assets, alter behavior, or provide a path to internal systems. Root access in the default image increases the potential impact but is not the only concern. A non-root process with production secrets is still valuable to an attacker.

Observed exploitation in KEV does not mean every LiteLLM instance was compromised. It means an exposed deployment should be treated as high priority and that patch completion should be paired with a credential and activity review where exposure cannot be ruled out.

The GitHub advisory lists litellm from 1.81.8 up to, but not including, 1.83.10. The advisory text recommends 1.83.11 or later after replacing the hand-rolled sandbox with RestrictedPython. Package metadata lists 1.83.10, creating a release-identification conflict. The assurance baseline should therefore be 1.83.11 or later unless a specific alternate artifact has direct vendor evidence.

Scope includes container images, Python packages, embedded gateways, managed services, and automation that can call the management API. Include development and data-science environments when they can reach production credentials or networks.

ZoomEye Search for app="LiteLLM" returned 92,332 product fingerprints on 2026-11-20. The CVE Filter returned 0. The product observation is the Exposure value but not a count of vulnerable systems. External data cannot show the endpoint route, master-key use, package version, or process user.

Use the external list as an unverified discovery source. Match it to owned services, then replace the external guess with local evidence. A zero CVE filter result should be recorded as index coverage, not as a safety conclusion.

Define four acceptance checks. First, the deployed artifact must be 1.83.11 or later or otherwise proven fixed. Second, POST /guardrails/test_custom_code must be blocked or reachable only through an approved administration path. Third, the workload must not expose unnecessary secrets, mounts, capabilities, or network reach. Fourth, administrative access and master-key use must be reviewed for the exposure period.

Assign an owner for each gateway and a date for each check. Collect version output, image digest, endpoint test results, process identity, secret references, and network policy evidence. Record exceptions with the compensating control and its owner. Do not close a ticket based only on a successful deployment pipeline message.

After patching, repeat inventory reconciliation and sample the running containers. Review requests to the test route, unexpected process activity, provider credential use, and changes to routes or guardrails. Keep a small post-incident record that states what was verified, what remains uncertain, and when the next inventory check will run.

#9931. How to reduce L3 support escalations: From ticket to tested fix

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Solve the biggest challenges in your codebase.

Most of the bugs that support escalates to L3 aren’t impossible for these engineers to resolve. But, L1 and L2 support engineers often lack the context and visibility into the code to resolve them on their own.

Support can see the symptom, the customer and the logs. The explanation of why a bug or regression occurred usually lies one step past where they sit, in a code path, a recent deploy or a config change. So the ticket climbs from L1 to L2 to L3 until it reaches one of the few senior engineers who can grok it.

Better routing won't change that. What changes is connecting that ticket to the same context that L3 has, then carry it through investigation, a proposed fix and a test before it lands on an engineer’s desk.

We've covered how to get from a support ticket to a root cause. This guide picks up where that one leaves off: what happens between the root cause and the merged fix, and how to keep your team in the loop.

Tickets reach L3 because it's the only tier that can connect what a customer saw to the code that caused it. Support tiers are meant to sort problems by difficulty. In practice, they sort them by visibility.

The ticket, the account and the help center

Behavior that only makes sense in the code

The code, deploy history and architecture

Nowhere, which is why everything ends up here

Distributed systems make it worse. A failure that spans two services and last week's deploy reads as noise in the logs and only becomes clear in the code, so L2 has little choice but to escalate.

An escalation simply hands the ticket off. It rarely includes everything the last person learned. Each handoff resets the investigation: the engineer re-reads the ticket, re-pulls the logs and investigates the same questions that support already asked the customer. Three tiers can mean three investigations of one bug.

That's why reshuffling the tiers doesn't stick. An L2.5, a triage rotation or a new on-call schedule changes who gets the ticket. It doesn't change what they can see when it arrives, or what the ticket brings with it.

PlayerZero approaches this with an engineering world model: one connected record of code, tickets, telemetry and deploy history, built from context graphs. Support, QA and engineering all work from that same record, so the context doesn't reset when the ticket changes hands.

The engineering teams cutting escalations fastest treat the ticket as a workflow with stages. Each stage has one job, and a person approves the stages that change anything outside the investigation.

In PlayerZero this maps directly to a workflow: a versioned, multi-stage pipeline where each stage either moves on automatically or waits for approval. Every organization starts with an L1 Support template out of the box (in addition to Engineering Scoping, PR Review, QA Testing, SRE Alert Response, and more). You can also require human approval before an agent writes to an outside system, such as updating a Jira or Zendesk ticket, or pushing a commit, while investigation continues in parallel without waiting.

One support engineer put it this way: "I don't really have to go into detail into the ticket. I just have to drop it into PlayerZero."

Not every stage needs someone watching it. Reading tickets, pulling logs and tracing code paths can't break anything, so let those run on their own. Here’s when someone should step in:

The second kind is easy to miss, especially once workflows start automatically on new tickets. Nobody is kicking off each run by hand anymore, so nobody is naturally watching for one to stop.

Here's how our team builds in PlayerZero to keep runs moving:

Test a new support workflow on closed tickets first. You already know the right answer, so you can judge the workflow's investigation against it before it touches a live issue.

One support team began with a handful of tickets it had already investigated by hand. Comparing the agent's root cause with the known one showed them where the workflow needed more context before they rolled it out further.

When support can carry a ticket to a tested fix, escalations stop being the default and become the exception.

Zuora shows it most clearly. After moving L3 investigation onto PlayerZero, L3 triage dropped from 3 days to 15 minutes, and escalations fell from 28 to 3 a month. Cyrano Video cut the engineering hours spent on support by 80%, and its customer success team now resolves 40% of issues without escalating. Cayuse resolves issues 80% faster and catches 90% of them before customers do.

#9929. HNSW vs cosine similarity: one is a metric, the other is an index, and what approximate search costs in recall

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at aliahmed.si

"HNSW vs cosine similarity" compares two different kinds of thing. Cosine similarity is a metric: it scores how close two vectors are (on normalised vectors, it's just their dot product). HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) is an index: a data structure that finds the vectors with the highest similarity without scoring every vector in the collection. You use them together: an HNSW index built for the cosine metric. The real choice is exact search vs approximate search: exact search scores everything and is always right; an approximate index scans a fraction and occasionally misses a true top result. That miss rate is measured as recall\@k. Below, tested NumPy code shows the trade-off: in my test, scanning 6% of the vectors gave 89% recall\@10, and scanning 25% gave 97%.

```python title="ann.py: exact" import numpy as np

def normalize(x): return x / np.linalg.norm(x, axis=-1, keepdims=True)

def exact_top_k(index: np.ndarray, query: np.ndarray, k: int = 10) -> np.ndarray: """Cosine similarity is a dot product on unit vectors; exact search scores every vector.""" scores = index @ query top = np.argpartition(-scores, k)[:k] return top[np.argsort(-scores[top])]

Note that the index still ranks candidates by cosine similarity. The metric doesn't change; only how many vectors get scored does.

#9928. What Is Futures Earn and How Does It Work for Traders?

MEXC Learn is an educational platform that helps users understand crypto trading, blockchain basics, and Web3 concepts.

MEXC Learn is an educational platform that helps users understand crypto trading, blockchain basics, and Web3 concepts.

MEXC Learn is an educational platform that helps users understand crypto trading, blockchain basics, and Web3 concepts.

Futures traders often keep spare stablecoins in their accounts for margin and new entries, and those funds may not earn interest. Futures Earn may allow eligible balances to accrue interest without leaving the account, while those funds remain available for trading.

Quick answer: Futures Earn is an exchange feature that pays interest on eligible balances in a futures account while the funds stay available for trading. Actual earnings depend on the APR, eligible principal, minimum balance requirements, principal caps, and platform-specific conditions.

Futures Earn is an interest product built into the futures account. Once switched on, supported assets in that account, usually stablecoins such as USDT, earn interest automatically. Depending on the platform, qualifying funds may stay in the futures account rather than being locked in a separate savings product, allowing them to remain available for trading.

Keep the two income streams apart: interest comes from holding an eligible balance, while trading profit or loss comes from your positions. You can earn interest while your trades lose money, and it will not cover those losses.

Supported assets, rates, and eligibility rules vary by exchange.

The amount that earns interest is the interest-bearing principal, which is not always your full balance. Some platforms determine eligible principal using balance snapshots, so it can differ from your real-time balance.

Some programs require a minimum balance and set principal caps above which additional funds earn nothing. Base interest and bonus interest may also have different caps.

APR (annual percentage rate) is an annualized rate; the examples below use simple interest without assuming compounding. Unlike APR, annual percentage yield (APY) accounts for compounding.

The base APR may apply without an open position, while qualifying positions can unlock a bonus APR.

For example, MEXC's futures earn program combines interest on eligible futures balances with potential position-based bonuses. The applicable rate depends on the account's eligibility and product conditions.

A higher advertised APR does not necessarily mean higher earnings. Position requirements, principal caps, and the length of time funds remain eligible can all affect the actual payout.

Some exchanges take balance and position snapshots, check eligibility, then calculate interest.

The calculation frequency and distribution schedule depend on the platform. Some products calculate interest hourly and credit it daily, while others follow different settlement rules.

Withdrawals, smaller positions, or lower eligible balances can reduce future earnings.

A simple estimate uses this formula when the same principal qualifies for the full APR:

Estimated Daily Interest = Eligible Principal × APR ÷ 365

For example, assume 10,000 USDT of eligible principal at 5% APR:

However, base and bonus interest may apply to different principal amounts. A more precise estimate is:

Estimated Daily Interest = [(Base Principal × Base APR) + (Bonus Principal × Bonus APR)] ÷ 365

Here, bonus APR means the additional rate, not the combined total.

Suppose 10,000 USDT qualifies for 5% base APR, but only 2,000 USDT qualifies for an additional 15% APR. Estimated daily interest would be:

[(10,000 × 5%) + (2,000 × 15%)] ÷ 365 ≈ 2.19 USDT

These are illustrative calculations, not quotes for a specific account. They assume unchanged principal and rates throughout the calculation period. Actual payouts depend on applicable caps, qualifying periods, balance snapshots, and settlement rules.

MEXC Futures Auto-Earn lets eligible users earn interest while trading futures, with qualifying balances remaining available as margin.

The November 2026 upgrade highlights USDT and USDE. Users should check the rates and conditions displayed in their own accounts before activating the feature.

Log in to your MEXC account and open Futures Earn from the Earn menu.

Check supported assets, minimum balances, personalized APRs, principal caps, and bonus tiers.

MEXC's November 3, 2026 USDT offer advertises a 5% base APR for eligible balances of at least 100 USDT, plus these position-based bonuses:

●       1,000 USDT position value: +1% APR

The highest tier brings the advertised total to 20% APR. However, MEXC's June 8 update introduced personalized APRs and separate principal caps for base and bonus interest. Actual account rates may differ.

The November 2026 USDE offer also advertises a 4.75% base APR.

Position value determines your bonus tier, not your interest-bearing principal. Holding 5,000 USDT while maintaining a 100,000 USDT qualifying position does not mean 100,000 USDT earns interest.

MEXC determines qualifying exposure using net futures position values averaged across snapshots. Coin-M Futures, USDCUSDT, Copy Trading, Grid Trading, Event Futures, and sub-account positions are excluded under its published FAQ.

Users must meet Primary KYC and regional eligibility requirements. Certain restricted regions, account types, or compliance conditions may prevent participation.

Read the product agreement and enable the feature. Transfer supported assets to your futures account if needed. Qualifying balances then begin accruing interest according to product rules.

Check credited interest in your distribution records, monitor your eligible principal and APR, and manage your positions as usual.

On MEXC, interest is calculated hourly and distributed the following day. Rewards are credited to the Spot account before being automatically transferred to the Futures account.

MEXC may automatically disable Futures Earn if an account triggers risk-control reviews or compliance restrictions.

MEXC, LBank, and MGBX offer interest-earning features for futures account balances, but their rates, requirements, and distribution methods differ.

The table summarizes published program details rather than guaranteed returns. Advertised APRs are not directly comparable unless the user qualifies for the relevant rates and earning limits.

What Should Traders Compare Before Choosing?

●       Effective APR: The rate you realistically qualify for, not the highest advertised rate.

●       Eligibility and earning caps: VIP levels, supported assets, minimum balances, and principal limits.

●       Trading flexibility and settlement: Whether funds remain usable as margin and when interest is credited.

The highest advertised APR does not always produce the highest earnings, especially when strict position requirements or principal caps apply.

Futures Earn is often presented as crypto futures passive income, but weigh both sides first.

●       Extra interest on eligible balances that would otherwise sit idle

●       Better capital efficiency, since qualifying funds remain available for trading

●       Automatic calculations and payouts after activation

●       Potential access to higher APR tiers through qualifying positions

●       Variable APRs, principal caps, and eligibility restrictions

●       Volatility, leverage, and liquidation losses exceeding interest earnings

●       Trading fees and perpetual funding payments reducing overall returns

●       Platform custody, operational, and compliance risks

Futures Earn interest does not offset or prevent trading losses. Opening a position just to unlock a bonus tier can cost more than it pays. Reviewing funding rates, open interest, and liquidation data can provide additional context about leveraged market conditions.

Both offer interest on eligible crypto holdings, but they operate differently.

Funds may remain usable for futures trading

Depends on subscription and redemption rules

Can I earn interest without opening a futures position?

Yes. On MEXC, eligible USDT balances earn base APR without an open position. Bonus APR requires qualifying positions.

Does Futures Earn affect my futures trading?

Not directly. Trading remains available, but margin requirements may limit transfers, and moving funds out can reduce interest.

No. APRs may change based on market conditions, eligibility, principal caps, and platform policies.

What happens to Futures Earn if my position is liquidated?

Liquidation can reduce your eligible principal and bonus APR eligibility. On MEXC, remaining eligible balances may continue earning interest.

Futures Earn offers a way to earn interest on eligible futures balances without stopping normal trading. Before activating it, compare realistic interest against trading risks, fees, principal caps, and eligibility conditions.

If you use MEXC, review the latest product terms and the actual rates available to your account before participating.

#9927. Meilisearch for Beginners: Search That Feels Instant

Users expect search to work like Google: type two letters, get results, typos forgiven. Building that with a SQL LIKE query is painful. Meilisearch is an open-source search engine, written in Rust, that gives you typo-tolerant, instant search with almost no configuration.

You send it documents, and it indexes them:

That typo tolerance is built in, along with ranking, faceted filtering, and highlighting of matched words. There is no schema to define and no mapping to tune — Meilisearch figures out the fields from your documents.

For a frontend, you can query Meilisearch directly from the browser with a search-only API key, or proxy it through your backend. It also has official SDKs for JavaScript, Python, Go, and more, and a hosted cloud option if you do not want to run the server yourself.

Meilisearch is for developers adding search to a blog, a store, a docs site, or a dashboard — anywhere a database LIKE query is too slow and Elasticsearch is too much. If your users search for things in your app, this is one of the fastest ways to make that search feel great.
