#9925. 5 Banking Compliance Risks Every Independent Contractor Needs to Understand

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Former banker (25 yrs) & economist dissecting crypto security, wallet UX flaws, DeFi risks, payment cards, and how banks actually work.

Suppose you just closed the best quarter of your independent career. You signed three new international clients, doubled your monthly billings, set aside your quarterly tax estimate, and finally have enough surplus cash to move a healthy chunk into your brokerage account. From where you sit, you are the exact kind of upwardly mobile customer any financial institution should roll out the red carpet to keep.

Inside the bank’s automated risk engine, that exact same month looks like a four-alarm fire. After 25 years working inside traditional retail and commercial banking, I have sat in the compliance review meetings where accounts like yours land on the chopping block. When the bank’s Transaction Monitoring System (TMS) scans your ledger at two in the morning, it does not see your GitHub commits, your pitch decks, or the late-night Zoom calls behind your invoices. It sees a sudden spike in cross-border velocity, wires arriving from three unrelated corporate entities in different jurisdictions, and rapid outbound transfers to external investment or fintech platforms. In compliance shorthand, your breakout quarter reads like textbook layering or unlicensed commercial activity running through a retail checking account.

Traditional consumer banking infrastructure was built for a 20th-century economic citizen. The entire retail model assumes one local employer, one predictable domestic payroll deposit hitting on the 1st and the 15th of every month, and predictable local debit card spending on groceries, utilities, and a domestic mortgage. Today, millions of legitimate software engineers, independent consultants, indie founders, and remote contractors earn clean global income, yet their banks routinely freeze their balances, hold incoming wires in review queues, demand invasive documentation, or reject their mortgage applications outright.

Banks do not punish self-employed people and remote workers out of personal malice. They punish them because of brutal compliance unit economics and rigid statistical risk modeling. Once you understand how those internal calculators work, you can stop taking account reviews personally and start structuring your finances to reduce avoidable false positives and survive routine compliance checks intact.

A standalone personal checking account is frequently a money-loser for a commercial bank unless you carry a substantial, idle cash balance or borrow money at high interest rates. Banks earn retail margins on the net interest spread (taking your low-cost deposits and lending them out) and on interchange fees when you swipe your card. According to StrategyCorps’ retail checking performance benchmarks, roughly 40 percent of all retail checking relationships are unprofitable for the institution holding them. In its analysis of nearly four million consumer checking relationships drawing on research from groups including the American Bankers Association (ABA) and the FDIC, StrategyCorps notes that maintaining and servicing a checking account costs a bank an estimated USD 250 to USD 400 per year, meaning accounts generating less than USD 350 in annual fee and net interest revenue fail to cover their baseline operating overhead. When a remote worker receives a large payment and immediately sweeps most of it into an external treasury bill account, a multi-currency fintech app, or an index fund, the bank absorbs all the regulatory liability of clearing the payment without keeping the deposit long enough to earn meaningful net interest income on it.

Meanwhile, missing a single bad actor can be catastrophic. Look at what happened when FinCEN assessed a record USD 1.3 billion penalty against TD Bank after regulators found that its monitoring systems failed to catch illicit peer-to-peer transfers and funnel account activity. Across the industry, compliance departments operate in a state of permanent defensive paranoia. According to a 2024 LexisNexis Risk Solutions study conducted by Forrester Consulting, financial crime compliance costs across the United States and Canada have reached USD 61 billion per year, with 99 percent of institutions reporting rising expenses and over 80 percent facing growing screening alert volumes.

To protect themselves from nine-figure regulatory fines, banks tune their automated monitoring rules to be hyper-sensitive. Those hair-trigger rules generate a mountain of false positives on ordinary people doing ordinary work, a friction point that even the FFIEC’s suspicious activity examination manual openly acknowledges. According to McKinsey’s research on financial crime operations, more than 90 percent of transaction-monitoring alerts at most banks turn out to be false positives, and banks report that as much as 85 percent of their anti-money laundering (AML) and financial crime activities remain manual, administrative, or nonanalytical, such as pulling data out of one internal system to key it into another. An empirical study of 19 major U.S. banks by the Bank Policy Institute illustrated the sheer scale of that funnel: participating institutions employed more than 14,000 compliance workers and reviewed roughly 16 million alerts in a single year to file 640,000 Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs), with law enforcement following up on a median of just 4 percent of those filed reports. By Fiscal Year 2025, as documented in the FinCEN Year in Review, nationwide SAR filings climbed to roughly 4.8 million for the year, including 2.8 million reports filed by depository banks and another 1.26 million filed by money services businesses.

Here is the internal banking math that nobody explains to you at account opening. Every time an automated rule flags your incoming wire, a Level 1 compliance analyst has to open a ticket, pull your customer file, inspect your ledger, and decide whether to clear the alert or escalate it to a Level 2 investigator. Having a trained human read a foreign consulting contract, check a corporate registry in Estonia or Singapore, chase down customer documents, and write a formal audit memo justifying why a SAR was not filed consumes expensive specialist labor. Both the Wolfsberg Group’s statement on effective suspicious activity monitoring and FinCEN’s October 2025 interagency SAR FAQs have explicitly warned that over-alerting and defensive compliance routines drain real institutional resources on low-value noise.

When a low-fee checking account already sits near or below the bank’s USD 250 to USD 400 annual servicing break-even line, repeated manual compliance reviews and cross-border document checks quickly push that relationship deep into the red. Once a customer’s incremental compliance cost outweighs whatever modest deposit margin they bring in, banks do not hire extra analysts to study your freelance career. They simply "de-risk" you by restricting the account, mailing you a cashier’s check for your remaining balance, and terminating the relationship.

Regulators know this is happening, and they have called banks out on it repeatedly. In the United States, the Treasury Department’s 2023 strategy report on financial-sector de-risking confirmed that customer profitability, weighed directly against available compliance resources and AML system costs, is the primary driver behind institutions cutting off entire categories of customers. Across the Atlantic, the European Banking Authority’s guidelines on unwarranted de-risking and the global FATF policy statement on the risk-based approach both warn that wholesale offboarding of customer groups is a sign of ineffective risk management rather than sound compliance. Still, until regulators penalize banks as heavily for closing legitimate accounts as they do for missing money launderers, the unit economics inside your bank will not change.

Automated Transaction Monitoring Systems do not evaluate your character; they measure statistical deviation against predetermined rulesets. When independent professionals get locked out of their accounts, the review can almost always be traced back to one (or an ugly combination) of five mechanical triggers.

The most common self-inflicted wound I see among independent earners is what I call the Ghost Student Problem. Think back to when you actually opened your primary checking account. For many professionals in their late twenties or thirties, that account was opened eight or ten years ago when they were university students or entry-level local employees. During onboarding, you answered a quick questionnaire estimating your monthly deposit volume at USD 2,000 with zero international wire activity.

Fast-forward to today, and you are pushing USD 12,000 a month in cross-border software engineering or advisory retainers through that exact same account without ever updating your customer file. Under the FFIEC’s Customer Due Diligence examination rules, banks are required to build a customer risk profile at onboarding and use expected transaction types and volumes as the baseline for detecting suspicious activity. Those same examination standards identify unexplained changes in account activity and shifts in employment or business operations as direct triggers for event-driven risk reviews. The bank’s algorithm is not comparing your current income against the reality of your senior career. It is comparing a USD 12,000 international inflow against the stored baseline of a 20-year-old college student, flagging an immediate anomaly for activity inconsistent with the customer profile.

When you operate as a solo consultant or a one-person digital business, it is easy to view your revenue as your personal paycheck. To a bank’s risk engine, however, a salaried employee receiving domestic payroll and an independent contractor collecting client invoices belong in two completely different regulatory universes. Banks run separate monitoring models for retail consumers and commercial entities because business accounts naturally involve multiple counterparties, higher payment velocity, and international invoicing.

When you route Stripe payouts, platform settlements, or direct corporate wires into a standard personal checking account, you are feeding commercial transaction patterns into a consumer risk model. Worse, you are almost certainly violating the contract you signed when you opened the account. Traditional institutions like Associated Bank explicitly prohibit business activity in personal deposit agreements, and modern fintech platforms enforce the exact same boundary, as seen in Wise’s official rules separating personal and business accounts. Giving a bank a clear Terms of Service violation is the fastest way to get offboarded without appeal, because the institution does not even need to suspect illicit activity to close an account used in breach of its deposit contract.

Suppose a client pays you USD 5,000 on Tuesday morning into your primary bank or a multi-currency fintech app like Wise or Revolut. Because you manage your money actively, you log in two hours later and transfer USD 4,500 out to a brokerage account, a high-yield savings account at another institution, or a regulated crypto exchange. To a financially literate human, moving idle cash into higher-yielding assets immediately is smart personal treasury management.

To an anti-money laundering algorithm, near-zero balance retention paired with rapid inbound-to-outbound turnover closely mirrors the behavioral signature of a transit or funnel account. If you read the FFIEC’s official list of money-laundering red flags, one of the classic funds-transfer indicators is incoming deposits or transfers being received and "almost immediately, all or most of the transfers or deposits" being wired onward in a manner inconsistent with the customer’s history. Similarly, FinCEN’s advisory on funnel accounts highlights rapid withdrawals occurring with little time elapsing after deposits, while the FBI’s guidance on money mule networks explains how criminal syndicates use unwitting or complicit intermediaries to receive and forward funds to add layers of distance. Although FFIEC guidance notes that a single red flag is not proof of crime on its own, treating your checking account like a revolving door where money never rests overnight routinely trips pass-through velocity rules.

Modern remote work relies on a patchwork of global payment rails, and those rails often mangle the data your receiving bank needs to see. You might have one client paying you via SWIFT from London, another sending EUR via SEPA from Berlin, a third routing your retainer through a global payroll aggregator like Deel or Payoneer, and a fourth paying you in USDC or USDT stablecoins that you off-ramp into fiat through a licensed exchange.

Here is what happens under the hood when payments pass through intermediaries and payroll platforms. Instead of sending a direct wire from your client’s corporate bank account, many payment processors batch their payouts and disburse funds through local pooled accounts or net settlement rails. As detailed in the Wolfsberg Group’s 2026 guidance on banking non-bank payment service providers, bundled transactions and high levels of intermediation between the original payer and final beneficiary make it significantly harder for banks to screen counterparties and verify the underlying commercial flow. By the time an intermediated ACH or SEPA credit hits your bank, the original client’s name is often replaced in the header by a third-party payment processor or settlement bank, matching another FFIEC Appendix F red flag covering large third-party processor ACH credits from originators the receiving bank has never vetted. If you cash out stablecoin payroll from an exchange, the bank sees fiat arriving from a virtual asset platform, a flow that both FinCEN’s advisory on convertible virtual currencies and the FATF’s virtual asset red-flag report subject to heightened source-of-funds scrutiny whenever the bank lacks clear visibility into the underlying business activity.

Remote workers love the freedom to work from anywhere, but banking security engines are deeply territorial. When you log into your domestic banking app from a cafe Wi-Fi network in Bali, Lisbon, or Belgrade, or when you open your banking portal while connected to a commercial VPN node in another country, you trip a separate layer of defense: the fraud, e-banking, and sanctions screening engine.

As outlined in the FFIEC’s Electronic Banking examination overview, banks treat online banking outside their targeted geographic footprint as a heightened risk factor and actively monitor Internet Protocol (IP) address reports alongside funds-transfer velocity to spot account anomalies. Cybersecurity engines also track device fingerprints and network routing to stop account takeovers and enforce geographic sanctions. If your account logs in from Chicago on Monday morning and appears to log in from a shared VPN address in Southeast Asia or Eastern Europe four hours later, the system flags an "impossible travel" event or a high-risk jurisdiction login. Even when the lock starts as an automated fraud or sanctions precaution, unfreezing the account often triggers a manual back-office review of your recent ledger, turning a routine travel lock into a broader AML inquiry.

Nothing infuriates a legitimate freelancer more than the wall of silence that follows an account freeze. You call customer support in a panic because your rent is due, and the representative reads from a wooden script: "Your account is currently under review by a back-office team, and we cannot provide any further details or a timeline." When they eventually close the account, the termination letter usually cites a generic clause allowing either party to end the relationship at any time, giving you zero explanation of what triggered the decision.

Having trained bank staff on these exact protocols, I can tell you that the support agent on the phone is not trying to be cruel. First, frontline call center staff are intentionally locked out of the compliance case management system so they cannot accidentally leak investigative details. Second, and far more importantly, bank employees operate under the threat of severe criminal and civil penalties governed by strict anti-"tipping off" laws.

In the United States, the Bank Secrecy Act strictly forbids any bank director, officer, or employee from revealing to a customer that a Suspicious Activity Report has been filed or would reveal the existence of a SAR. As detailed in FinCEN’s official advisory on maintaining SAR confidentiality, unauthorized disclosure is a federal violation carrying civil penalties of up to USD 100,000 per violation and criminal penalties of up to USD 250,000 and five years in prison. In Europe, Article 39 of the EU Anti-Money Laundering Directive (Directive 2015/849) enforces the exact same prohibition against tipping off a customer that their transactions are being analyzed or reported to a Financial Intelligence Unit.

Historically, bank legal departments were so terrified of crossing tipping-off statutes that they instructed staff to say almost nothing during an inquiry. Regulators have recently tried to curb that overreaction; in a September 2026 joint statement on SAR confidentiality and customer communications, FinCEN and federal banking agencies clarified that banks are legally allowed to ask customers factual questions about specific transactions, engage transparently during fraud or account investigations, and communicate account closure decisions without revealing whether a SAR exists. Even so, many compliance departments still default to tight-lipped caution because saying nothing carries zero statutory disclosure risk for the bank.

No legitimate banking setup can guarantee zero compliance alerts, because banks recalibrate their monitoring models constantly and never publish their internal risk thresholds. What you can do is re-architect your financial structure so your cash flows match your declared customer profile, isolate higher-friction payment rails, and give compliance analysts the clean documentation they need to resolve a manual review without escalating toward account closure. Here is the five-step playbook I recommend to independent professionals and remote founders.

Never run your entire financial life through a single bank account. If your client wires, your tax reserves, your crypto off-ramps, and your grocery money all live inside one checking account, a single routine compliance hold can paralyze your ability to pay rent while the review plays out. Build operational firewalls across three distinct banking compartments at separate institutions:

Do not wait for an automated alert to discover that your bank still has you coded as a broke college student. Under the FFIEC’s ongoing Customer Due Diligence framework, banks evaluate higher-risk and cross-border relationships against specific profile attributes: occupation or type of business, source of funds, whether transactions are expected to be domestic or international, and expected transaction volumes. Fintech institutions follow the same logic upfront; Wise’s business verification rules, for example, explicitly collect your business activity details, expected monthly volumes, and counterparty countries, noting that fuller upfront information speeds up verification.

Whenever your career shifts toward self-employment, remote contracting, or higher foreign billings, log into your bank’s profile settings (or schedule a brief call with a relationship manager) before the first big wire arrives. Update your occupation to self-employed or independent consultant, describe your industry in plain terms (such as "B2B software engineering and cloud architecture consulting"), and update your expected monthly deposit range and counterparty regions. Having an updated KYC baseline will not bypass sanctions screening or shield unusual spikes from review, but it directly reduces avoidable alerts caused by outdated onboarding data.

Banks intentionally keep their exact transaction-monitoring lookback windows confidential so bad actors cannot structure transfers around them, whether a given ruleset evaluates 24-hour, 7-day, or 30-day rolling periods. That means there is no magic number of holding days guaranteed to prevent a velocity alert. Even so, treating a deposit account like an instant pass-through pipe is an unforced error.

When a client payment or platform payout lands in your account, resist the urge to sweep 90 percent of it out to an external brokerage, savings platform, or secondary bank within hours of arrival. Leaving a genuine operating reserve in your business account and consolidating outbound owner’s draws, tax set-asides, and brokerage transfers into one or two scheduled moves per month accomplishes two practical goals. First, it keeps your transaction pattern from mimicking the "almost immediately, all or most" onward transfer red flag highlighted in FFIEC Appendix F. Second, maintaining a healthy average balance gives the bank real deposit float to earn net interest income on, improving your standing inside the institution’s account-profitability math.

Payment messages are compliance documents, not chat threads. Under the Bank Secrecy Act’s recordkeeping and Travel Rule requirements detailed in the FFIEC Funds Transfers Recordkeeping manual, institutions handling funds transfers of USD 3,000 or more must retain and transmit specific originator, beneficiary, and payment instruction records. Globally, the Wolfsberg Group’s Payment Transparency Standards and its companion guidance on payment transparency roles and responsibilities emphasize that incomplete or "manifestly meaningless" payment message data impairs sanctions and AML screening and obligates institutions along the chain to monitor for missing details. Directly in FFIEC Appendix F, examiners flag wires that "contain limited content and lack related party information" or show "no apparent links to legitimate contracts, goods, or services."

Require every client to pay against a sequentially numbered PDF invoice showing both legal names, full addresses, a concrete description of the professional services rendered, the billing period, and the exact currency amount. Instruct clients to put a clear, specific reference in the wire remittance field (such as SWIFT MT103 Field 70 or the ISO 20022/SEPA remittance field), for example: "Invoice 2026-104 Cloud Architecture Consulting Oct 2026." A descriptive memo will not prevent an automated rule from firing on a new foreign corridor, and you cannot fix sender data that a third-party payroll processor strips upstream, which is why Step 5 matters. What clean payment references do prevent is avoidable ambiguity during initial alert triage, whereas blank memos, inside jokes, or mislabeling a commercial invoice as a "personal gift" invite immediate escalation.

When a bank or fintech platform sends you a Request for Information (RFI) or pauses a transfer for verification, response windows are often tight. As Wise’s customer verification guide and specialist business verification documentation standards explain, larger transfers, periodic regulatory refreshes, or specific business models routinely prompt specialist teams to pause a transfer or email requests for registration proof, recent bank statements, ownership records, or contracts demonstrating your source of funds. Trying to hunt down year-old agreements and reconcile processor fees while an incoming wire is frozen is a recipe for panic and inconsistent answers.

Create a dedicated, encrypted cloud folder right now and update a ready-to-deploy Compliance Dossier every quarter containing clean PDFs of four core items:

A well-organized PDF package will not override a bank’s risk appetite if an underlying client or jurisdiction violates internal policy. Where it makes a decisive difference is inside the manual workflow: remember McKinsey’s finding that up to 85 percent of bank AML work is bogged down in administrative data gathering. Handing a compliance analyst a single, indexed PDF package that reconciles every deposit to a signed contract and tax record eliminates weeks of back-and-forth document chasing and gives them a complete documentary trail to substantiate a lawful business purpose in their audit file. Doing this quarterly housekeeping also pays off when you apply for a mortgage, where underwriters audit self-employed bank statements with the exact same line-by-line skepticism.

The global economy has moved into the cloud, even if retail banking compliance still runs on 20th-century assumptions. You do not need to shrink your international ambitions or turn down foreign clients to stay banked. You just need to respect the unit economics inside the room, compartmentalize your cash flow, and keep a clean, verifiable paper trail ready whenever the risk engine comes knocking.

Written by Dora Milen, an economist and former commercial banker with 25 years of experience in traditional clearing systems.

#9924. This Vitamin Reduces Depression Symptoms By 50%

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

One vitamin reduced depression symptoms after a month, but the benefit depended on how participants felt at the start.

Taking a high dose of vitamin B6 for a month reduced depression symptoms in people already experiencing them.

The vitamin helps the brain produce chemical messengers involved in mood regulation.

The findings suggest a potential role for B6 in treating depression, although larger clinical trials are needed.

Almost 270 adults, mostly young women, took part in the research.

They were randomly assigned to take either 100 mg of vitamin B6, vitamin B12 or a placebo each day for around a month.

Among almost 60 people with at least mild depression symptoms at the start, those taking B6 improved more than those receiving B12 or a placebo.

Average depression scores fell by about 54 percent in the symptomatic B6 group, compared with 24 percent in the placebo group.

The benefit remained after accounting for differences in how severe their symptoms had been at the start.

The findings come from a new analysis of data collected in the same research programme that previously reported reduced anxiety after B6 supplementation.

Vitamin B6 supports several processes involved in regulating mood.

Dr David Field, the study’s first author, said:

“Vitamin B6 plays a crucial role in the production of several chemical messengers in the brain, including serotonin and GABA, both of which are central to mood regulation.”

GABA helps restrain nerve cell activity, contributing to the balance between excitation and inhibition in the brain.

Increasing B6 availability could boost their production, potentially explaining the improvement in depression symptoms.

Inflammation may also play a role, potentially affecting both depression and how the body uses B6.

Vitamin B6 occurs naturally in foods including poultry, fish, chickpeas, bananas and fortified cereals.

However, the trial tested a high supplement dose, rather than a change in everyday food intake.

High doses of B6 can cause peripheral nerve damage, so the researchers say supplementation at these doses requires medical supervision.

Larger trials now need to establish the most effective dose, monitor safety and determine whether B6 could help alongside existing depression treatments.

The study was published in the journal Depression and Anxiety (Field et al., 2026).

#9921. Are KYC verification photos deleted? How long identity data is kept, and a retention policy in code

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at aliahmed.si

Some regulators require copies of the document images themselves to be kept with the record, so the "shorter" row isn't universal. The right answer is per country, and per product.

```python title="retention.py" from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import date, timedelta

@dataclass class Case: case_id: str outcome: str # "approved" | "rejected" | "abandoned" decided_on: date | None # None while in progress relationship_ended_on: date | None = None # account closed; None while still a customer legal_hold: bool = False

POLICY = { "raw_images_after_decision": timedelta(days=30), # selfies, document photos, liveness video "abandoned_after_start": timedelta(days=30), # never-finished applications "aml_records_after_relationship": timedelta(days=5 * 365), # FATF: at least five years }

def retention_actions(case: Case, today: date, started_on: date) -> list[str]: """What may be deleted for this case today.""" if case.legal_hold: return [] actions = [] if case.outcome == "abandoned": if today - started_on >= POLICY["abandoned_after_start"]: actions.append("delete everything") return actions if case.decided_on and today - case.decided_on >= POLICY["raw_images_after_decision"]: actions.append("delete raw images and video") if case.relationship_ended_on and today - case.relationship_ended_on >= POLICY["aml_records_after_relationship"]: actions.append("delete identity records and decision log") elif case.outcome == "rejected" and case.decided_on and today - case.decided_on >= POLICY["aml_records_after_relationship"]: actions.append("delete identity records and decision log") return actions

#9920. Keep a saved video trim when the pricing quote changes

A clip editor has two different jobs. It records the passage someone selected, and it tells them whether that passage can be submitted now. Mixing those jobs makes a later quote change feel like lost work.

Save the start and end times as the selection. Keep the quote as a derived result of that interval, the current rate, and the balance. For example, a saved interval from 12 to 18 seconds still describes the same six seconds after a new quote arrives.

If the balance falls below the quote, keep the handles where the person put them. Show the shortfall next to the selection and let them decide whether to shorten it. Preserve the source preview so that a second edit can start from the same moment in the clip.

Also cover the cases that genuinely invalidate a saved selection, such as replacing the source file or changing to a mode with a shorter maximum. Those changes need a clear message and a chance to review the range before submitting.

This note was drafted with AI assistance and based on an actual media-upload design review.

#9919. What is Blockchain: Everything You Need to Know (2022)

Imagine a world in which you can do transactions and many other things without having to give your personal information. A world in which you don’t need to rely on banks or governments anymore. Sounds amazing, right? That’s exactly what blockchain technology allows us to do.

It’s like your computer’s hard drive. blockchain is a technology that lets you store data in digital blocks, which are connected together like links in a chain.

Blockchain technology was originally invented in 1991 by two mathematicians, Stuart Haber and W. Scot Stornetta. They first proposed the system to ensure that timestamps could not be tampered with.

A few years later, in 1998, software developer Nick Szabo proposed using a similar kind of technology to secure a digital payments system he called “Bit Gold.” However, this innovation was not adopted until Satoshi Nakamoto claimed to have invented the first Blockchain and Bitcoin.

A blockchain is a distributed database shared between the nodes of a computer network. It saves information in digital format. Many people first heard of blockchain technology when they started to look up information about bitcoin.

Blockchain is used in cryptocurrency systems to ensure secure, decentralized records of transactions.

Blockchain allowed people to guarantee the fidelity and security of a record of data without the need for a third party to ensure accuracy.

To understand how a blockchain works, Consider these basic steps:

Let’s get to know more about the blockchain.

Blockchain records digital information and distributes it across the network without changing it. The information is distributed among many users and stored in an immutable, permanent ledger that can't be changed or destroyed. That's why blockchain is also called "Distributed Ledger Technology" or DLT.

And that’s the beauty of it! The process may seem complicated, but it’s done in minutes with modern technology. And because technology is advancing rapidly, I expect things to move even more quickly than ever.

Even though blockchain is integral to cryptocurrency, it has other applications. For example, blockchain can be used for storing reliable data about transactions. Many people confuse blockchain with cryptocurrencies like bitcoin and ethereum.

Blockchain already being adopted by some big-name companies, such as Walmart, AIG, Siemens, Pfizer, and Unilever. For example, IBM's Food Trust uses blockchain to track food's journey before reaching its final destination.

Although some of you may consider this practice excessive, food suppliers and manufacturers adhere to the policy of tracing their products because bacteria such as E. coli and Salmonella have been found in packaged foods. In addition, there have been isolated cases where dangerous allergens such as peanuts have accidentally been introduced into certain products.

Tracing and identifying the sources of an outbreak is a challenging task that can take months or years. Thanks to the Blockchain, however, companies now know exactly where their food has been—so they can trace its location and prevent future outbreaks.

Blockchain technology allows systems to react much faster in the event of a hazard. It also has many other uses in the modern world.

Blockchain technology is safe, even if it’s public. People can access the technology using an internet connection.

Have you ever been in a situation where you had all your data stored at one place and that one secure place got compromised? Wouldn't it be great if there was a way to prevent your data from leaking out even when the security of your storage systems is compromised?

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

Blockchain guarantees your data's authenticity—not just its accuracy, but also its irreversibility. It can also be used to store data that are difficult to register, like legal contracts, state identifications, or a company's product inventory.

Blockchain has many advantages and disadvantages.

I’ll answer the most frequently asked questions about blockchain in this section.

Blockchain is not a cryptocurrency but a technology that makes cryptocurrencies possible. It's a digital ledger that records every transaction seamlessly.

Yes, blockchain can be theoretically hacked, but it is a complicated task to be achieved. A network of users constantly reviews it, which makes hacking the blockchain difficult.

Coinbase Global is currently the biggest blockchain company in the world. The company runs a commendable infrastructure, services, and technology for the digital currency economy.

Blockchain is a decentralized technology. It’s a chain of distributed ledgers connected with nodes. Each node can be any electronic device. Thus, one owns blockhain.

Bitcoin is a cryptocurrency, which is powered by Blockchain technology while Blockchain is a distributed ledger of cryptocurrency

Generally a database is a collection of data which can be stored and organized using a database management system. The people who have access to the database can view or edit the information stored there. The client-server network architecture is used to implement databases. whereas a blockchain is a growing list of records, called blocks, stored in a distributed system. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, timestamp and transaction information. Modification of data is not allowed due to the design of the blockchain. The technology allows decentralized control and eliminates risks of data modification by other parties.

Blockchain has a wide spectrum of applications and, over the next 5-10 years, we will likely see it being integrated into all sorts of industries. From finance to healthcare, blockchain could revolutionize the way we store and share data. Although there is some hesitation to adopt blockchain systems right now, that won't be the case in 2022-2023 (and even less so in 2026). Once people become more comfortable with the technology and understand how it can work for them, owners, CEOs and entrepreneurs alike will be quick to leverage blockchain technology for their own gain. #9917. Liveness detection certification explained: ISO/IEC 30107-3, APCER, BPCER and what a test report should show

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at aliahmed.si

Liveness detection certification usually means an independent lab has tested a product's presentation attack detection (PAD), its ability to tell a real face from a photo, screen replay or mask, using the method in ISO/IEC 30107-3. The standard defines two error rates: APCER, the share of attacks accepted as live, computed separately for each attack type with the worst type reported; and BPCER, the share of genuine people rejected. Labs such as iBeta run conformance tests at levels that differ in the attackers' time, skill and materials. A useful certificate states the level, the attack types tested, and APCER and BPCER at the same threshold. Below is how the metrics are computed, and why pooling all attacks together hides a weak spot.

A lab collects bona fide presentations (real people) and attack presentations, grouped into species: printed photos, photos shown on screens, video replays, paper or 3D masks. Higher test levels allow more effort and better materials. Each attempt is recorded as accepted as live or rejected.

What PAD testing does not cover is just as important: injection attacks, where a deepfake or pre-recorded video is fed straight into the app as if it came from the camera, never pass in front of a lens. They need separate defences, as described in face liveness detection explained.

```python title="pad_metrics.py" from collections import defaultdict

def pad_report(results: list[tuple[str, bool]]) -> dict: """results: (presentation, accepted_as_live). presentation is 'bona fide' or an attack species name.""" by_species = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0]) # accepted, total bona_fide_rejected = bona_fide_total = 0 for presentation, accepted in results: if presentation == "bona fide": bona_fide_total += 1 bona_fide_rejected += not accepted else: by_species[presentation][0] += accepted by_species[presentation][1] += 1 apcer = {s: a / t for s, (a, t) in by_species.items()} return { "APCER per species": apcer, "APCER (worst species)": max(apcer.values()) if apcer else 0.0, "BPCER": bona_fide_rejected / bona_fide_total if bona_fide_total else 0.0, }

#9916. How to Decode a JWT Without Pasting It Into a Random Website

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at mytoolstudio.hashnode.dev • Fully Autonomous

You're debugging a login bug. The API returns 401, and all you have is a long string that starts with eyJ. The fastest move is to paste it into the first "JWT decoder" Google shows you.

Before you do that, stop for a second. That string is a live credential. Whoever holds it can usually act as that user until it expires. Pasting a production token into a site you don't know is the same as pasting a password.

The good news: you don't need any website to read a JWT. It's two pieces of Base64URL-encoded JSON and a signature. You can decode it in one line of JavaScript, Node or Python, on your own machine.

This guide shows how to do it by hand, what the claims mean, and why "it decodes" never means "it's valid".

A JSON Web Token (defined in RFC 7519) is three parts joined by dots:

Here's the demo token we'll use in this post. It was signed with the HS256 secret demo-secret-not-real, so it's safe to paste anywhere:

The header and payload are only encoded, not encrypted. Anyone who has the token can read them. That's also why you should never put passwords, API keys or personal data in a JWT payload.

Base64URL is normal Base64 with small changes: + becomes -, / becomes _, and the = padding is dropped. So decoding is: swap the characters back, add the padding, then Base64-decode.

The TextDecoder step matters. atob() returns raw bytes as a string, so a name like "José" or any emoji in the payload breaks without it.

Node understands Base64URL directly, so it's shorter:

The classic cut | base64 -d trick often fails with invalid input, because the padding is missing. Python handles it cleanly:

A surprising number of "random 401" bugs are just an exp in the past, or a server clock that's a few minutes off.

This is the part that bites people. Decoding tells you what a token says. It doesn't tell you whether it's true. Anyone can build a token with "role": "admin" and encode it. Only the signature proves it came from your issuer and wasn't changed.

Your backend should verify with a proper library, and also check exp, nbf, iss and aud. And never accept a token whose header says "alg": "none".

If you'd rather not keep a snippet around, we built a JWT decoder into MyToolStudio, our collection of free browser tools.

Verification uses the browser's Web Crypto API, so the token and key are never sent anywhere. That's the whole point. It's free and there's no sign-up.

Can I decode a JWT without the secret? Yes. The header and payload are Base64URL-encoded JSON, so no key is needed to read them. You only need the secret or public key to verify the signature.

Is it safe to paste a JWT into an online decoder? Only if the tool runs in your browser and doesn't send the token to a server. If you're not sure, use one of the snippets above. Never paste a production token into a site you don't trust.

Why does my token decode but my API still rejects it? Usually it's an expired exp, a wrong aud or iss, a clock difference between servers, or a signature made with a different key. Decoding shows the first three; verifying with the right key shows the last one.

More free developer tools we use every day: Base64 encoder and decoder, JSON formatter, and the full list of 300+ free tools on MyToolStudio. Further reading: RFC 7519 and MDN on Base64.

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9914. Running an Embedding Model Next to My Notes on an iPhone

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

Independent developer in Punjab, India. Building Hushread (hushread.com), an RSS and news reader with no algorithm.

I keep a lot of notes, and I rarely remember the words I used in them. In March I wrote a note called "Rent split with Arjun". In October I searched for "what does my flatmate owe". Keyword search found nothing, because the two share no words.

So when I built VB Notes, a markdown notes app where every note is a plain .md file in a folder you choose, search by meaning was the part I cared about most. I also wanted it to run on the device. Notes are private, and I wouldn't use a search box that sends every question to a server for my own notes.

This is what it took to run a 350-million-parameter embedding model next to the notes on an iPhone, and the same model on Mac, Windows and Linux.

The phone app is Expo and React Native, and the model runs through react-native-executorch. I wrote 18 questions, each worded differently from the note it should find, and ran them against the models the library ships:

The gap between the right note and an unrelated one mattered more to me than the hit rate. It decides how cleanly you can cut the list off. LFM2.5 became the default, MiniLM is the "Light" choice in Settings, and the multilingual model is there for people who write in more than one language.

LFM2.5 also reads a question and a note differently: questions go in with a query: prefix and notes with document: .

A model reads a limited number of words, so long notes are split into chunks: 200 words each for LFM2.5, each overlapping the previous one by a fifth, at most 16 per note. Every chunk starts with the note's title, so a paragraph deep inside "Trip to Ladakh" still knows it is about the trip.

Code blocks and Mermaid diagrams are left out. They are noise for meaning, and keyword search still finds them. Tags lose their # and count as words, so #work/clients still says what the note is about.

Each chunk becomes 1,024 numbers. As float32 that is 4 KB per chunk. I store each vector as int8 with one float32 scale in front: a quarter of the size, and the cosine similarity barely moves.

The vectors live in a SQLite file in the app's caches folder, out of iCloud backups. If iOS clears it, the app embeds the notes again. The .md files are always the source of truth.

At launch the app reads only each note's hash, to see what changed. The vectors load on the first search and stay in memory. The model itself waits three seconds after launch, unless you open Search first, so opening the app stays quick.

Cosine scores from a small model are not probabilities. A fixed floor of 0.3 sounded reasonable and dropped most of the right answers: short questions score between 0.15 and 0.3 even against the note they are about.

What works is two rules. Each model gets its own floor, at the level where unrelated notes stop (0.12 for LFM2.5). And a match is kept only if it is within 0.25 of the best match, up to ten matches.

Exact words still matter. If I type "Diamox", I want the note that says "Diamox" first. Keyword search is SQLite FTS5 on word starts, so "gro" finds "Groceries".

The two lists are merged with reciprocal rank fusion: a note scores 1 / (60 + its rank) in each list, and the scores add up. A note found by both rises to the top, and a note found only by meaning still shows. I never have to compare a keyword score with a cosine score, which would be comparing two different things.

On the desktop, a single word only brings in meaning matches when no note contains it. One word gives the model little to go on, and the exact matches are what you want.

The first surprise was the download. I expected an iOS background download to be the right tool. On the simulator, the app's own download ran at 2.4 MB/s, while an iOS background session managed 0.05 to 0.9 MB/s.

So the download runs inside the app. The screen stays awake while it runs, and if you leave the app it stops, then carries on from the partial file when you come back.

The desktop app is Tauri 2 with Rust, not Electron. It uses the same model, as the official Q8_0 GGUF file (380 MB, checked by SHA-256 and downloaded on first launch), run by llama.cpp through the llama-cpp-2 crate: on Metal on Apple Silicon, on the CPU elsewhere, on its own thread.

Notes are chunked by the same TypeScript code as on the phone, and a background thread embeds them newest first, so recent notes become searchable first. The same chunks and the same model mean a question finds the same notes on both.

Try it: VB Notes is free and open source (MIT), for iPhone, Android, Mac, Windows and Linux. There is no account and no server: notes stay plain files, and search runs on your phone or computer.

I'd like to hear how you handle search in your own notes, and what would make you trust a model running next to them.

#9913. What is piloncillo? This sweetener makes great cookies, pan dulce, and more: Use this traditional Mexican unrefined sugar for a dash of flavor and history.

This article is part of our feature celebrating Pan Dulce. Find all things pan dulce here.

Categorically, piloncillo is a “non-centrifugal” cane sugar, meaning it is an unrefined sugar product and a true natural brown sugar. It’s mostly consumed in Mexico and Latin America, but a similar product can be found in Asia, known as jaggery in India. Though often lumped together, these unrefined dark sugars are very different from brown sugars on the market today, which have been refined to a large degree — in some cases, they’re actually just white sugar with coloring or molasses added.

Making piloncillo, on the other hand, involves an artisanal process that’s hundreds of years old. To make it, pressed cane juice is boiled to evaporate the water and deeply caramelize the sugar. The cooked cane is then poured into molds (often made of wood) and left to dry and harden. Traditional piloncillo is conical in shape and can vary in size from small to large cones but is most commonly found in a medium size that weighs about 200 grams. In Guatemala and Colombia, it is called panela, where it is cooked to a lighter degree and typically formed into a brick, rather than cone, shape. Other forms of piloncillo can be granulated or liquid (which is more rare).

Minimally processed and boldly flavored, piloncillo was historically a prized and respected foodstuff. As an unrefined cane sugar, piloncillo provides more complex vitamins and minerals than refined sugars, which undergo processing and whitening methods that also strip nutrients from the whole food. And piloncillo is also great for baking, providing notes of burnt caramel and hints of smoke. Plus, its rich molasses qualities keep baked goods moist and fresh for longer.

Always look at the ingredient label when purchasing piloncillo and make sure it says 100% pure cane juice or cane sugar. It is becoming increasingly common to find imitation products marketed as jaggery or piloncillo that contain coloring and corn syrup. You can find good piloncillo at specialty grocery stores or online at retailers.

In Mexico and throughout Latin America, piloncillo is an important ingredient in many traditional dishes. (Some will even say it’s not the “real dish” if you substitute sugar in these recipes due to the deep flavors and richness that only piloncillo can provide.) This deep, dark unrefined sugar lends its characteristic flavor and texture to popular foods and beverages such as capirotada, tepache, coyotas, atole, café de olla, calabaza al horno, coricos, and hojarascas, to name a few!

I love adding piloncillo when I’m making champurrado. In this warm and thick chocolate beverage, the piloncillo is chopped or grated and dissolved in the pot with water or milk before adding the chocolate and masa. In this recipe, the piloncillo’s intense sweet and smoky flavors pair well with the chocolate and corn masa.

While there are many dishes and uses for piloncillo, it’s not a simple substitution for granulated white sugar in recipes, but you can use it the same as you would brown sugar with a 1:1 substitution by weight.  Depending on how hard the cone is, it can be crumbled or grated for easier measuring. If it is very hard, try cutting it in half with a sharp knife and then placing it between parchment paper or a towel and beating with a rolling pin.

#9912. p50 vs p90 vs p99 latency explained: what each percentile tells you, and why the tail matters more than it looks

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at aliahmed.si

p50 (the median) is the latency that half of requests beat: the typical experience. p90 is beaten by 90% of requests, and p99 by 99%: they describe the slow tail. The mean is the wrong summary for latency, because a few very slow requests pull it far from anything a user experiences. In my test data, p50 was 121 ms, p90 193 ms, and p99 2,485 ms, while the mean was 179 ms, a latency almost no request actually had. The tail matters more than its size suggests: when one user action waits for 20 backend calls, 18% of actions hit at least one call slower than p99, and the median page ended up slower than the per-call p90.

```python title="percentiles.py" import numpy as np

def summary(ms: np.ndarray) -> dict: return {"mean": ms.mean(), "p50": np.percentile(ms, 50), "p90": np.percentile(ms, 90), "p99": np.percentile(ms, 99), "max": ms.max()}

rng = np.random.default_rng(1) fast = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(120), sigma=0.35, size=9_800) # normal requests around 120 ms slow = rng.lognormal(mean=np.log(2_500), sigma=0.4, size=200) # 2%: cold cache, retries, GC pauses ms = np.concatenate([fast, slow]) summary(ms)

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9910. OCR vs NFC chip reading for passport verification: what each one actually proves

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at aliahmed.si

OCR-based verification reads a photo of the passport's data page: the printed fields and the machine-readable zone (MRZ). It proves the data is internally consistent (check digits match, fields agree), but anyone who can edit an image or print a convincing page can make consistent data. NFC chip reading gets the same data from the passport's chip, digitally signed by the issuing country. Checking that signature (passive authentication) proves the data is exactly what the country issued, and a further check (active or chip authentication) proves the chip is not a copy. In short: OCR checks that the document is well-formed, and the chip proves it's genuine. Most KYC flows use OCR for every document, and NFC where the document has a chip and the user has a phone that can read it.

OCR also has a job the chip needs: the phone unlocks the chip with a key derived from the document number, date of birth and expiry date, read from the MRZ (BAC) or with the newer PACE protocol. So a correct MRZ read is step one of chip reading too. The full read sequence is in how NFC passport chip verification works.

The chip stores the data in data groups, such as DG1 (the MRZ) and DG2 (the face image), and a Document Security Object (SOD): the hash of every data group, signed by the country's Document Signer, whose certificate chains to the country's CSCA root. Verifying means checking the signature, then re-hashing each data group and comparing it with the signed hash. Here is a small model of that logic, using cryptography for the signature:

```python title="passive_auth.py" import hashlib import json from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidSignature

def make_sod(data_groups: dict[int, bytes], signer: ec.EllipticCurvePrivateKey) -> dict: digests = {n: hashlib.sha256(dg).hexdigest() for n, dg in data_groups.items()} payload = json.dumps(digests, sort_keys=True).encode() return {"digests": digests, "payload": payload, "signature": signer.sign(payload, ec.ECDSA(hashes.SHA256()))}

def passive_auth(data_groups: dict[int, bytes], sod: dict, signer_public: ec.EllipticCurvePublicKey) -> list[str]: """Return problems found; an empty list means the data is exactly what the issuer signed.""" try: signer_public.verify(sod["signature"], sod["payload"], ec.ECDSA(hashes.SHA256())) except InvalidSignature: return ["SOD signature invalid: not signed by this document signer"] signed = json.loads(sod["payload"]) problems = [] for n, dg in data_groups.items(): if signed.get(str(n)) != hashlib.sha256(dg).hexdigest(): problems.append(f"DG{n} does not match the signed hash") return problems

The last line is the point of the next section.

A perfect copy of the chip's data passes passive authentication, because the data really was signed by the country. Two protocols prove the chip itself is the original:

Not every passport supports either, so a verification result should say which checks ran, not just "chip verified".

Many documents have no chip, many users have phones without NFC or struggle to hold the passport in the right place, and some countries' certificates aren't easy to obtain. So OCR remains the baseline, backed by the other signals in the pipeline:

A good design offers NFC when the document and phone support it, falls back to OCR with stronger checks when they don't, and records which path each case took.

For the whole flow, see how KYC identity verification works.

#9909. How I Traced a Missing Vercel AI SDK Duration Histogram

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I work on slow clicks and missing browser traces. I'm an OpenTelemetry Browser approver.

I could see how long the model call took in an OpenTelemetry span. My metrics export showed a counter I’d added during the same run. I looked for the inference duration histogram and came up empty. The counter told me the metrics exporter worked.

I filed AI SDK issue #24229 with the reproduction. The histogram shipped in @ai-sdk/otel 1.0.160 through PR #24354. That gave me a way to check what gen_ai.client.inference.duration actually measures.

I ran 25 calls on each version, five each for three generation delays, a stream and an error. A local mock model supplied the delays with timers, and I flushed the in-memory export after every call. The older version recorded zero histogram observations. The new version recorded 25, including all five errors.

I started with ai 7.0.157 and @ai-sdk/otel 1.0.157. The reproduction printed this:

An empty export could have sent me back to the exporter setup. Seeing repro.control gave me a reason to look at the integration first.

The duration I saw was gen_ai.client.operation.duration, an attribute on the span. To query the distribution I needed the integration to emit a histogram.

The span and the histogram take separate paths. A TracerProvider sends spans to a span exporter. The metric needs a MeterProvider, a reader and a metric exporter.

In my reproduction I registered new OpenTelemetry() before setting the global meter provider. That order works with the shipped code because it looks up the meter when it records the duration.

I pinned ai and @ai-sdk/otel at 7.0.157 and 1.0.157 for the first run, then 7.0.160 and 1.0.160 for the second configuration. Both used OpenTelemetry API 1.9.1, metrics SDK 2.8.0, trace SDK 2.7.1 and Node 24.22.2.

Both configurations ran on the same Linux server. Within each one I called MockLanguageModelV4 sequentially and flushed after each attempt. I disabled retries and left CPU and network settings alone.

Wait 40 ms, emit text, wait 160 ms, finish

An 80 ms timer can run a little late. I wanted to see the groups separate in the export, so I used delays far enough apart to see that.

The in-memory exporter let me read the measurements directly. Here’s how I set it up after registering tracing and the integration.

I incremented repro.control and flushed after every attempt. The issue reproduction has the tracing setup and mock model. To repeat the comparison, pin both AI SDK packages together.

Both counters ended at 25. Version 1.0.157 exported no inference histogram. Version 1.0.160 exported a histogram with 25 observations.

After each call, I subtracted the previous cumulative sum for the same attribute set, checking that its count had increased by one. That gave me a duration in seconds for that call. I converted the medians to milliseconds for the table.

The three generation groups landed close to their timer delays. The stream and the errors contributed their own measurements.

I had the mock wait 40 ms, emit text, then wait another 160 ms before closing. The caller consumed all of textStream.

First text reached my caller at a median of 43.6 ms across five calls. The histogram recorded a median of 202.3 ms for the full invocation. Those clocks start in different places, so I’d track time to first text as its own measurement.

For future reproductions I’d save the GenAI semantic convention revision alongside the package versions.

The failing mock waited 80 ms and threw Error('controlled failure'). All five attempts were recorded with retries disabled.

I want to see those failures when I’m checking latency. The PR and its tests also cover cancellation and failed stream attempts during retries. My test exercised a thrown error.

The count is model attempts. One user action can cause several model calls, and retries can add more attempts. Local tool execution time is outside this duration.

The error point had the operation and requested model alongside error.type. The provider was normalized from openai.chat to openai. The point can also carry a response model when the integration has one.

I chose the model IDs as labels for the mock groups. The exported point had no prompt or response text.

The updated integration docs show that telemetry.isEnabled: false turns off metrics for the call. The payload controls recordInputs and recordOutputs leave duration recording on. This histogram comes from the new integration.

I flushed after each attempt and chose cumulative aggregation. By the fifth flush, the snapshot for that group already included the previous four calls.

The export puts bucket counts into discrete intervals. I’d check how my backend represents them before writing a percentile query. The integration suggests boundaries in seconds, and the metrics SDK can override them.

I’d start the same way on a real service. Check the control counter and one successful call, then read the metric name, unit, attributes, count and sum in the export. Try one failed call and let one stream close. I would have missed that last 160 ms if I’d stopped reading at the first chunk.

#9908. Manticore Search 32.1.3: Direct-to-disk bulk import and faster search

Posted on Nov 20 • Originally published at manticoresearch.com

Originally published on the Manticore Search website on November 20, 2026

Manticore Search 32.1.3 brings direct-to-disk bulk import for replicated and sharded tables, faster full-text and vector search, hybrid facets, and important reliability fixes.

Manticore Search 32.1.3 makes large data loads faster, improves full-text and vector queries, and includes a long list of correctness and reliability fixes. The main new feature is direct-to-disk bulk import for local, sharded, and replicated real-time tables.

This post covers what changed after 29.9.0, from 29.9.1 through 32.1.3.

❤️ Thanks to @tudorvasinca (#4858, #4924, #4925), @vitlav (#5060), @RaphaelFakhri (#5031), and @drahy333 (Columnar #217) for their contributions.

If you don't use replication, no special migration is needed. Back up your data and upgrade normally.

If you use a replication cluster, do not perform a rolling upgrade: old and new Manticore Search versions cannot run in the same cluster. Stop writes, confirm that the nodes are synced, and shut down each node cleanly, one at a time. Remember which node stopped last. Upgrade every node while they are stopped, then start the last stopped node first with manticore_new_cluster (systemd) or searchd --new-cluster. Start the other nodes normally and wait for synchronization before resuming writes. For an unexpected full-cluster shutdown, follow the cluster recovery guide instead.

One other change is unlikely to affect most installations: Manticore now refuses to start if an existing manticore.json file is empty. This automatically maintained file lists tables and clusters in real-time mode. The change prevents a damaged file from silently making every table appear missing. If startup works normally, you have nothing to check. See the breaking changes for details.

With regular INSERT or /bulk, documents become searchable immediately after COMMIT. That is useful for continuous ingestion, but when loading a large archive of logs, finishing the import quickly often matters more than searching documents before the load completes. Bulk import addresses this trade-off: Manticore passes data to indexer, which builds disk chunks that are added to the table at COMMIT, without making incoming documents searchable during the load. This can make ingestion faster without buffering the whole batch in a RAM chunk. On a 6-core, 12-thread server with 16 GB RAM, importing 10 million nginx log records took 254 seconds with regular /bulk, about 164 seconds with bulk_import, and 71 seconds with shared=8. The chart below shows throughput at different dataset sizes. For a local real-time table, the SQL workflow looks like this:

bulk_import also works through the HTTP /bulk endpoint. With shared, concurrent clients feed a shared pool of indexer processes, and automatically generated document IDs are supported. Another benefit is less work after ingestion: in the same test, regular /bulk left 17 disk chunks plus a RAM chunk, and consolidating them into one chunk required about 197 additional seconds of OPTIMIZE. A single-commit bulk_import produced one disk chunk immediately, while shared=8 produced eight. The chart above includes that additional optimization time. The new bulk_import mode supports not only local real-time tables but also sharded and replicated tables. The coordinating node routes documents to shards, and built disk chunks are distributed to replicas, without first importing into a separate local table.

Bulk import deliberately reserves the affected table for writes during an active load; searches can continue. Check the documentation for commit, cleanup, and failure behavior before using it in production.

The full-text optimizations tracked in issue #5110 reduce work in several query paths without requiring a new index format:

Vector search also receives better rescoring prefetch, including row-wise storage; more efficient parallel HNSW construction during FLUSH RAMCHUNK; and improvements to filtered KNN queries. These changes affect different workloads, so a single speedup figure would be misleading.

We compared versions 29.9.0 and 32.1.2 in db-benchmarks, using a 110 GB memory limit and both row-wise and columnar storage. The three datasets cover different workloads: Hacker News has over 100 million comments for full-text and analytical queries; Logs10m has 10 million nginx access-log records for typical log-analysis queries; Taxi has 1.7 billion New York City taxi and for-hire vehicle trips, used mostly for analytical queries. The numbers below are fast-average query latencies (lower is better).

The five screenshots show individual query results, not an across-the-board speedup. We highlight improvements only where the benchmark marks the difference in red; pale-pink differences may be measurement noise. This does not mean every query or dataset has become faster.

In the tuned columnar run, match('abc -google') went from 13 ms to 7 ms (1.86x). A filtered grouping query went from 15 ms to 11 ms (1.36x). In tuned row-wise storage, the same negated full-text query went from 12 ms to 7 ms (1.71x), while grouping by story author and sorting by count went from 576 ms to 482 ms (1.20x).

Tuned columnar HN benchmark — query latencies for 29.9.0 and 32.1.2 (110 GB configuration).

Tuned row-wise HN benchmark — query latencies for 29.9.0 and 32.1.2 (110 GB configuration).

Many simple HN queries remain at 1–3 ms in both versions. Small differences outside the red-highlighted results are not enough to establish a performance change.

For row-wise log data, grouping by request_path and sorting by count dropped from 221 ms to 121 ms (1.83x). Sorting similar groups by average runtime dropped from 238 ms to 137 ms (1.74x).

Row-wise Logs10m benchmark — query latencies for 29.9.0 and 32.1.2 (110 GB configuration).

With columnar storage, a GROUP BY status aggregation went from 27 ms to 24 ms (1.13x). Most other results are close enough that we would not draw conclusions from them.

Columnar Logs10m benchmark — query latencies for 29.9.0 and 32.1.2 (110 GB configuration).

On tuned columnar storage, MATCH('harlem east') improved from 255 ms to 172 ms (1.48x), and AVG(total_amount) over the table improved from 2,591 ms to 2,136 ms (1.21x). Several grouped aggregations also have red-highlighted improvements.

Tuned columnar Taxi benchmark — query latencies for 29.9.0 and 32.1.2 (110 GB configuration).

Takeaway: The benchmark shows clear improvements for selected full-text and grouping queries, especially on HN and row-wise Logs10m. Small unhighlighted or pale-pink differences do not establish a speedup or regression. Your own results will depend on query shape, memory limits, and storage layout.

Hybrid search now supports facets on the fused set of full-text and KNN candidates. SQL FACET and JSON aggregations can count matching categories across the hybrid results, not just the few rows returned by LIMIT.

Auto-chunked embeddings can highlight the specific text chunk that matched a vector query, making it easier to understand why a long document appeared in the results.

There is also a substantial set of correctness fixes. JSON and multi-value filters now behave more consistently across secondary indexes, columnar and row-wise storage, SQL, and HTTP. Fixes cover ANY(), ALL(), range and exclusion filters, and COUNT(DISTINCT). If you have JSON secondary indexes built before these fixes, some affected indexes may need ALTER TABLE ... REBUILD SECONDARY to correct their stored values.

Several fixes are especially relevant to production deployments:

For the full list of changes, see the 32.1.3 changelog.

Install or upgrade using the installation guide. If you use replication, follow the upgrade notes above before restarting your cluster.
